readme.markdown:
# Stripe MCP Server by Insightful Pipe

> **Connect Stripe to AI assistants: read-only payments, subscriptions, invoices and revenue data.**

Part of the [Insightful Pipe MCP Server Collection](https://insightfulpipe.com/mcp-servers) — use Stripe from Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, and other AI assistants through the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

## MCP Server URL

```
https://stripe.insightfulmcp.com/
```

## What is Stripe MCP?

Stripe MCP is a **remote Model Context Protocol server** hosted by InsightfulPipe. Access payments, subscriptions, invoices, customers, charges, refunds, and financial data from your Stripe account.

## Installation

### Claude

1. Copy the MCP Server URL: `https://stripe.insightfulmcp.com/`
2. Open [Claude Connectors Settings](https://claude.ai/settings/connectors)
3. Scroll to the bottom and click **Add custom connector**
4. Paste the URL and click **Add**
5. Click **Connect** and sign in to InsightfulPipe if asked. Claude then lists the connector as connected.

### ChatGPT

Custom MCP servers are added through ChatGPT's **Developer mode**. Availability depends on your ChatGPT plan, and workspace admins may need to allow it.

1. Turn on **Developer mode** in ChatGPT settings
2. Create a new app for a remote MCP server and paste the URL: `https://stripe.insightfulmcp.com/`
3. Sign in to InsightfulPipe if asked. The connection finishes as soon as you are signed in.

See OpenAI's guide: [Developer mode and MCP apps in ChatGPT](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/12584461-developer-mode-and-mcp-apps-in-chatgpt)

### Claude Code

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http stripe https://stripe.insightfulmcp.com/
```

### Cursor

Add the server to `~/.cursor/mcp.json` (all projects) or `.cursor/mcp.json` (one project):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "stripe": {
      "url": "https://stripe.insightfulmcp.com/"
    }
  }
}
```

When Cursor shows **Needs authentication**, click **Connect** and sign in to InsightfulPipe if asked.

## Available Actions

41 actions: 41 read, 0 write.

### Read Actions (41)

<details>
<summary>Show all 41 read actions</summary>

| Action | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `get_account` | Retrieve the current account details |
| `get_accounts` | List all connected accounts (Stripe Connect) |
| `get_application_fees` | List all application fees collected from connected accounts (Connect) |
| `get_balance` | Retrieve the current account balance (available, pending, and connect reserved amounts by currency) |
| `get_balance_transactions` | List balance transactions (funds movements: charges, refunds, transfers, payouts, etc.) |
| `get_charge` | Retrieve a specific charge by ID |
| `get_charges` | List all charges |
| `get_checkout_sessions` | List all Checkout Sessions |
| `get_coupons` | List all coupons |
| `get_credit_notes` | List all credit notes |
| `get_customer` | Retrieve a specific customer by ID |
| `get_customers` | List all customers |
| `get_dispute` | Retrieve a specific dispute by ID |
| `get_disputes` | List all disputes (chargebacks) |
| `get_early_fraud_warnings` | List all early fraud warnings from Radar |
| `get_events` | List events (webhooks log) |
| `get_file_links` | List all file links |
| `get_files` | List all files uploaded to Stripe (dispute evidence, identity documents, etc.) |
| `get_invoice` | Retrieve a specific invoice by ID |
| `get_invoice_items` | List all invoice items (line items that can be added to invoices) |
| `get_invoices` | List all invoices |
| `get_payment_intent` | Retrieve a specific payment intent by ID |
| `get_payment_intents` | List all payment intents |
| `get_payment_methods` | List payment methods for a specific customer |
| `get_payout` | Retrieve a specific payout by ID |
| `get_payouts` | List all payouts |
| `get_plans` | List all plans (legacy pricing model, prefer Prices) |
| `get_prices` | List all prices |
| `get_product` | Retrieve a specific product by ID |
| `get_products` | List all products |
| `get_promotion_codes` | List all promotion codes |
| `get_refund` | Retrieve a specific refund by ID |
| `get_refunds` | List all refunds |
| `get_reviews` | List all Radar reviews |
| `get_setup_intents` | List all setup intents |
| `get_shipping_rates` | List all shipping rates |
| `get_subscription` | Retrieve a specific subscription by ID |
| `get_subscription_schedules` | List all subscription schedules |
| `get_subscriptions` | List all subscriptions |
| `get_top_ups` | List all top-ups |
| `get_transfers` | List all transfers |

</details>

## Control What Your AI Can Do

You decide what AI agents can do with each connected account:

- **Turn individual actions on or off** for every connected account, so agents only see the actions you allow.
- **Connect as Read-only or Read & Write.** A read-only connection can only enable read actions.
- **Destructive actions stay off by default.** Actions such as deletes are disabled until an admin enables them.
- **Team access per account.** Restricted team members only use the accounts they are granted, with the read actions enabled on them.

## Usage Examples

```
"What is my current Stripe balance?"
```

```
"How many active subscriptions do we have?"
```

```
"List failed payments from the last 7 days"
```

## Pricing

The Stripe MCP server is included in every InsightfulPipe plan, together with all other MCP servers and the CLI. Plans start at $29.99/month, and you can try it for 7 days. See [insightfulpipe.com/pricing](https://insightfulpipe.com/pricing) for current plans.

## What is Slack MCP?

Slack MCP is a **remote Model Context Protocol server** hosted by InsightfulPipe. Access channels, messages, users, conversations, and search across your Slack workspace.

## Installation

### Claude

1. Copy the MCP Server URL: `https://slack.insightfulmcp.com/`

    "postgresql": {
      "url": "https://postgresql.insightfulmcp.com/"
    }
  }
}
```

When Cursor shows **Needs authentication**, click **Connect** and sign in to InsightfulPipe if asked.

## Available Actions

8 actions: 7 read, 1 write.

### Read Actions (7)

| Action | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `analyze_db_health` | Report database health (connections, vacuum age, replication slots, cache hit rates, invalid constraints) |
| `explain_query` | Return the EXPLAIN plan for a query |
| `get_table_metadata` | Full metadata for a table or view: columns, constraints, indexes, estimated row count, size |
| `get_table_schema` | Return the column list (name, data_type, is_nullable, default) for a table or view |
| `get_top_queries` | Slowest or most resource-intensive queries from the pg_stat_statements extension |
| `list_schemas` | List all schemas in the connected database |
| `list_tables` | List tables, views, sequences, or extensions in a schema |

### Write Actions (1)

| Action | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `run_query` | Execute a SQL statement against the connected database |

## Control What Your AI Can Do

You decide what AI agents can do with each connected account:

- **Turn individual actions on or off** for every connected account, so agents only see the actions you allow.
- **Connect as Read-only or Read & Write.** A read-only connection can only enable read actions.
- **Destructive actions stay off by default.** Actions such as deletes are disabled until an admin enables them.
- **Team access per account.** Restricted team members only use the accounts they are granted, with the read actions enabled on them.

The open-source browser agent. Run it locally with any LLM, or on [Browser Use Cloud](https://cloud.browser-use.com): stealth browsers from $0.02/hour, top score (90.5%) on [Stealth Bench V2](https://browser-use.com/benchmarks/browsers).

# Navigate the web like a human does.

Find an available slot, pick a date and time, handle the CAPTCHA, and book a driving test.

[Explore more demos and prompts ↗](https://browser-use.com/showcase)

> **AI agents and crawlers:** read [browser-use.com/llms.txt](https://browser-use.com/llms.txt) for the product map (open source, Browser Harness, Cloud browsers, Agents API, pricing) and [docs.browser-use.com/llms.txt](https://docs.browser-use.com/llms.txt) for the documentation index. Browser Use is the open-source browser agent (Python and TypeScript), a $0.02 per browser-hour cloud browser with stealth, CAPTCHA solving and residential proxies, and a hosted agent API.

# Which Browser Use do I need?

  
  
  
  

- **[Path 1: Fully Hosted Cloud](#path-1-fully-hosted-cloud):** Scale up with a fully hosted agent and browser.
- **[Path 2: CLI](#path-2-cli):** Automate your own browser tasks.
- **[Path 3: Python Library](#path-3-python-library):** Run the open source Browser Use agent locally from your own code.

# Quickstart

## Path 1: Fully Hosted Cloud

Scale browser automation with our hosted agent, stealth browsers, and infrastructure for profiles, recordings, and data policies.

[Get started with the API ↗](https://docs.browser-use.com/cloud/agent/quickstart)

New Google, GitHub, or Microsoft signups get **$1 cloud credit**.

## Path 2: CLI

Paste this prompt into Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, OpenClaw, or your favorite agent.

```text
Install or upgrade browser-use to the latest stable version with uv using Python 3.12, run `browser-use skill install` to register the skill, and connect it to my browser. If setup or connection fails, follow https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.
```

## Path 3: Python Library

Run the Browser Use agent locally from Python, with your choice of model and a local or cloud browser:

**1. Install Browser Use (Python >= 3.11):**

With [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/) installed, run `uv init --python 3.12` first if you're starting a new project.

```bash
uv add browser-use
```

**2. Add your [OpenAI API key](https://platform.openai.com/api-keys) to `.env`:**

```bash
# .env
OPENAI_API_KEY=your-key
# BROWSER_USE_API_KEY=your-key  # Optional: BU2 model or cloud browser
```

For either optional Browser Use service, get a [Browser Use API key](https://cloud.browser-use.com/new-api-key).

**3. Save this as `agent.py`:**

```python
import asyncio

from browser_use import Agent, Browser, ChatBrowserUse, ChatOpenAI
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv()

async def main():
    llm = ChatOpenAI(model='gpt-5.6-luna', reasoning_effort='xhigh')
    # llm = ChatBrowserUse(model='bu-2-0')  # Use BU2 instead; requires BROWSER_USE_API_KEY
    agent = Agent(
        task="Find the number of stars of the browser-use repo",
        llm=llm,
        # browser=Browser(use_cloud=True),  # Use a cloud browser; requires BROWSER_USE_API_KEY
    )
    history = await agent.run()
    print(history.final_result())

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

To use BU2, replace the `ChatOpenAI` line with the commented `ChatBrowserUse` line. The cloud-browser option works with either model.

**4. Run it:**

```bash
uv run agent.py
```

The agent opens a browser, looks up the repository, and prints its answer.

**5. Run the same agent on a cloud browser (no Chrome to install; works in Docker, CI, and serverless):**

Set `BROWSER_USE_API_KEY` ([get a key](https://cloud.browser-use.com/new-api-key?utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme-path3)), then uncomment the `browser=` line in `agent.py` and run it again:

```python
    agent = Agent(
        task="Find the number of stars of the browser-use repo",
        llm=llm,
        browser=Browser(use_cloud=True),
    )
```

Cloud browsers cost $0.02 per browser-hour plus network traffic ([pricing](https://browser-use.com/pricing)), and add stealth, residential proxies, CAPTCHA solving, and a live view URL. Same code, no other changes.

[Python library docs ↗](https://docs.browser-use.com/open-source/introduction)

Use Claude's browser toolset with Browser Use as the driver. Browser Use

readme.markdown:
# Kaiva Postgres MCP

The Postgres MCP server that stays read-only. A drop-in replacement for the archived
`@modelcontextprotocol/server-postgres`.

## Switch in one line

Where your AI client starts the archived server today:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "postgres": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-postgres", "postgresql://localhost/mydb"]
    }
  }
}
```

change the package name:

```json
      "args": ["-y", "@kaiva/postgres-mcp", "postgresql://localhost/mydb"]
```

In Claude Code:

```sh
claude mcp add postgres -- npx -y @kaiva/postgres-mcp postgresql://localhost/mydb
```

The `query` tool, its `sql` input and the table schema resources are the same, so nothing else
changes.

Other ways in, with `DATABASE_URL` set in your environment:

- Claude Code plugin: `/plugin install postgres-mcp --marketplace ai-kaiva/postgres-mcp`
- Gemini CLI extension: `gemini extensions install https://github.com/ai-kaiva/postgres-mcp`, then
  `gemini extensions config kaiva-postgres-mcp` to enter the database URL
- Docker: `docker run -i --rm -e DATABASE_URL ghcr.io/ai-kaiva/postgres-mcp` once the image is published

## Why switch

The archived server is no longer maintained: Anthropic archived it in 2025 as a reference example
rather than production software, and npm marks it "Package no longer supported". It runs whatever
text it is given inside `BEGIN TRANSACTION READ ONLY`, and that is not enough:

- `COMMIT; DROP SCHEMA public CASCADE` ends the read-only transaction and drops the schema
  (reported by Datadog Security Labs in August 2025; the fix never reached npm, where 0.6.2 is
  still the latest version).
- With a superuser login, which is what most local and Docker installs start with, one statement
  can run a shell command on the database server: PostgreSQL runs `COPY ... TO PROGRAM` inside a
  read-only transaction.

We checked both against version 0.6.2 on PostgreSQL 14: both ran. Kaiva Postgres MCP refuses both.

| | Archived 0.6.2 | Kaiva Postgres MCP |
|---|---|---|
| A second statement after `COMMIT` | Runs | Refused: one statement per call, and PostgreSQL itself refuses a second |
| `COPY ... TO PROGRAM`, server file reads, `dblink` | Run, if the login allows | Refused |
| Time limit | None | 15 seconds per statement, 3 seconds waiting for a lock |
| Rows returned | All of them | The first 1,000, and it says so |
| Superuser login | Used as given | Warning on this machine; refused for a database on another machine unless you allow it |
| Tables listed | `public` schema only | Every schema |
| Dates and timestamps | Turned into JavaScript dates, which can shift a date to the day before | Exactly as PostgreSQL prints them |
| Errors | Returned as protocol errors | Returned to the AI with what to fix |
| Maintained | No | Yes |

## Tools

- `query`: run one read-only SQL statement (`SELECT`, `WITH`, `VALUES`, `TABLE`, `SHOW` or
  `EXPLAIN`) and get the rows as JSON.
- `list_tables`: the tables and views this login can read, with type, estimated row count and
  comment.
- `describe_table`: one table's columns, primary key, unique and foreign keys, the tables that
  reference it, and its indexes.

Resources: each table's columns, as the archived server listed them.

## How read-only is enforced

On every call:

1. The SQL is checked before it is sent: one statement, starting with `SELECT`, `WITH`, `VALUES`,
   `TABLE`, `SHOW` or `EXPLAIN`, calling no function that reaches past the transaction (`dblink`,
   server file functions, `lo_import` and `lo_export`, `pg_terminate_backend`, advisory locks, and
   functions that run SQL given to them as text).
2. It runs alone, through PostgreSQL's extended query protocol, which refuses a second statement,
   inside a `READ ONLY` transaction with a statement time limit and a lock time limit.
3. The transaction is always rolled back, and `DISCARD ALL` resets the session, so nothing a
   statement sets up outlives it.

Only the first 1,000 rows are fetched from the database (one more is read, to know whether more
exist), so a query over a large table returns quickly.

## Use a login that can only read

The strongest guard is a login that cannot write. Run this once as an administrator, then put
`mcp_readonly` in the connection URL:

```sql
CREATE ROLE mcp_readonly LOGIN PASSWORD 'choose-a-password';
GRANT CONNECT ON DATABASE mydb TO mcp_readonly;
GRANT pg_read_all_data TO mcp_readonly;  -- PostgreSQL 14 and later
ALTER ROLE mcp_readonly SET default_transaction_read_only = on;
```

To see what a login can do:

```sh
npx -y @kaiva/postgres-mcp postgresql://mcp_readonly:...@localhost/mydb --check
```

## Options

| Option | Default | |
|---|---|---|
| `--max-rows <n>` | 1000 | Rows returned per query, 1 to 10000 |
| `--timeout <seconds>` | 15 | Time limit per statement, 1 to 300 |
| `--allow-superuser` | off | Allow a superuser login on a database on another machine. In Docker Compose the database is another container, so this applies there too; a read-only login is the better answer |
| `--check` | | Connect once, report what the login can do, and exit |

Give the connection URL as the first argument, or set `DATABASE_URL`. TLS settings go in the URL
(`sslmode`, `sslrootcert`), as with `psql`.

## What it does not protect

- Anything the login can read, the AI can read: tables, views and foreign tables, and with a
  superuser the system catalogs too (`pg_authid` holds password hashes). Use a login that sees only
  the tables you mean to share.
- The refused-function list is a second guard, not a sandbox. It sees the SQL the AI sends, not what
  a view, a foreign table (`file_fdw`) or a function already defined in your database does when it
  is read. With a superuser login such an object can still read a file on the database server. With
  a login that can only read, PostgreSQL itself refuses (checked: a view over `pg_read_file` reads
  the file as a superuser and is refused as a read-only login).
- "This mac

# SA Business Calendar MCP

Hosted [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server that gives AI agents exact South African business-day answers: public holidays (including Sunday-to-Monday observed days and once-off declared holidays), business-day maths, and SARS EMP201/VAT201 due dates.

**Get it on Apify Store → [apify.com/ali_mora/sa-calendar-apify](https://apify.com/ali_mora/sa-calendar-apify)**

## Tools

| Tool | What it does | Price |
|---|---|---|
| `is_business_day` | Is a date a weekend or SA public holiday? Returns the reason. | Free |
| `days_until_next_holiday` | Next SA public holiday after a date, and the days until it. | Free |
| `add_business_days` | Add or subtract SA business days, skipping weekends and holidays. | $0.01/call |
| `business_days_between` | Count SA business days between two dates. | $0.01/call |
| `holidays_in_range` | List SA public holidays between two dates. | $0.01/call |
| `next_sars_deadlines` | Next EMP201 and VAT201 due dates, adjusted for weekends and holidays. | $0.01/call |

Billed per call through Apify. Failed calls aren't charged.

## Connect

Endpoint (Streamable HTTP), authenticated with your [Apify API token](https://console.apify.com/account/integrations):

```
https://ali-mora--sa-calendar-apify.apify.actor/mcp
```

**Any MCP client:**

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "sa-business-calendar": {
      "url": "https://ali-mora--sa-calendar-apify.apify.actor/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer <APIFY_TOKEN>" }
    }
  }
}
```

**Claude Code:**

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http sa-business-calendar https://ali-mora--sa-calendar-apify.apify.actor/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer <APIFY_TOKEN>"
```

## Example prompts

- "Invoice dated 14 December 2026 on 5-business-day terms. When is it due?"
- "When are my next EMP201 and VAT201 payments due?"
- "List every SA public holiday between now and the end of March."

## Notes

- Dates are `YYYY-MM-DD`. National public holidays only; no provincial or bank-specific days.
- SARS rules are simplified (monthly VAT vendors). Verify against [sars.gov.za](https://www.sars.gov.za) before relying on them for filing.
- This repo holds the listing and registry metadata. The server source is private.

Issues and requests: open an issue here or on the Apify Store page.

readme.markdown:
# cam [English](README.md) · [中文](README.zh.md) · [日本語](README.ja.md) · [한국어](README.ko.md) · [العربية](README.ar.md) · [🌐 Website](https://hanochzhu.github.io/cam-web/?lang=en) ### A local multi-turn conversational memory system purpose-built for coding agents **Code graph + memory · surgical reads · 100% local · MCP + CLI** **Kernel written in Rust** ## Contents - [Why cam?](#why-cam) - [Get Started](#get-started) - [Key Features](#key-features) - [How It Works](#how-it-works) - [Agent Workflow](#agent-workflow) - [CLI Reference](#cli-reference) - [Memory Rules](#memory-rules) - [Configuration](#configuration) - [Benchmarks](#benchmarks) - [Supported Agents](#supported-agents) - [Supported Languages](#supported-languages) - [Supported Platforms](#supported-platforms) - [License](#license) Guides: [Interactive Showcase (Website)](https://hanochzhu.github.io/cam-web/?lang=en) · [Main Agent vs Subagent](docs/agents.md) · [MCP Configs by IDE](docs/mcp.md) · [中文说明](docs/agents.zh.md) --- ## Why cam? When an AI coding agent explores a repository, it usually rediscovers structure the slow way — running `grep`, `glob`, and full-file `Read` one file at a time — and forgets everything in the next session. **`cam` gives the agent two local retrieval planes in a single binary:** | Plane | What it stores | How the agent uses it | | --- | --- | --- | | **Code Graph** | Tree-sitter symbols (functions, types, methods) as a virtual filesystem + 1-hop callers/callees | `ls`, `find`, `read src/file.rs/symbol`, `ref symbol --dir in\|out` — surgical symbol reads instead of whole-file dumps | | **Memory Tree** | Project facts, architecture decisions, debugging write-ups, and user habits | `recall` (Vector + BM25 fused with RRF) and `add` (with branching `--parent` and revision `--supersedes`) | > **One binary, two interfaces:** The **main agent** calls `cam` over **MCP** (`cam mcp`); **subagents** (which rarely inherit MCP tools) call the exact same **CLI** (`cam --json …`). Both share `.cam/cam.db` on disk, 100% local, zero API cost. --- ## Get Started ### Option 1: One-Sentence Agent Install (Recommended) Paste this prompt directly into your coding agent (**Cursor**, **Claude Code**, **Codex**, **Windsurf**, **GitHub Copilot**, **Cline**, etc.) and let it install, index, and wire `cam` for you: ```text Install cam from https://github.com/HanochZhu/codeagent_memory: require a working Rust toolchain (rustup), run `cargo install --git https://github.com/HanochZhu/codeagent_memory --locked`, ensure ~/.cargo/bin (or %USERPROFILE%\.cargo\bin on Windows) is on PATH, then verify with `cam --help`. In this repo run `cam index`. For the main agent, register MCP stdio: command `cam`, args `["mcp"]` (Cursor: .cursor/mcp.json; Claude Code: .mcp.json). Subagents call `cam --json` in the shell. Do not add extra docs. ```
How each IDE / agent handles this prompt | Environment | What to do | | --- | --- | | **Cursor / Windsurf / Claude Code / Codex** | Paste into Agent / Chat; the agent runs the terminal install, builds `.cam/cam.db`, and writes the MCP config | | **VS Code** (Copilot / Continue / Cline) | Paste into Agent / Chat mode with terminal access enabled | | **JetBrains** (IntelliJ / RustRover / GoLand) | Paste into AI Assistant, or run `cargo install` in the built-in terminal | Note: `cargo install` places `cam` in `~/.cargo/bin` (Windows: `%USERPROFILE%\.cargo\bin`). Restart your terminal or IDE if `cam` is not immediately found on `PATH`.
--- ### Option 2: Manual Setup #### 1. Install the CLI Requires a [Rust toolchain](https://rustup.rs/): ```bash cargo install --git https://github.com/HanochZhu/codeagent_memory --locked cam --help ```
Alternative: Build from local clone or run via Docker **From a local clone:** ```bash git clone https://github.com/HanochZhu/codeagent_memory.git cd codeagent_memory cargo install --path . --locked ``` **Docker (no Rust toolchain required):** ```bash docker pull ghcr.io/hanochzhu/codeagent-memory:0.1.5 docker run -i --rm -v "$PWD:/work" -w /work ghcr.io/hanochzhu/codeagent-memory:0.1.5 ``` Or build locally: `docker build -t cam https://github.com/HanochZhu/codeagent_memory.git`
#### 2. Index & query your project ```bash cd your-project cam index # parse repo into .cam/cam.db # Query the code graph cam ls src/ # list files or symbols in a file cam read src/main.rs/main # read a single symbol body cam ref main --dir in # 1-hop callers (in) or callees (out) # Query & write to the memory tree cam recall "how does hybrid recall fuse BM25 and vectors" cam add --summary "..." < notes.md ``` `cam` auto-initializes `.cam/` on first use. Run `cam watch` in the background if you want live incremental graph updates as files change. #### 3. Connect MCP for the main agent Add `cam mcp` to your host's MCP configuration (e.g. `.cursor/mcp.json` or `.mcp.json`): ```json { "mcpServers": { "cam": { "command": "cam", "args": ["mcp"] } } } ``` See [docs/mcp.md](docs/mcp.md) for host-specific config paths and [docs/agents.md](docs/agents.md) for main-agent / subagent prompt rules. The first `recall` or `add` downloads the default embedding model (`potion-multilingual-128M` to `~/.cam/models/`) and falls back to a lexical hash embedder if offline. --- ## Key Features | Feature | Details | | --- | --- | | **SQLite Code Graph** | Tree-sitter parses functions, types, and call edges into `.cam/cam.db` for instant symbol-level navigation | | **Virtual Paths** | `src/main.rs` addresses a file outline; `src/main.rs/main` addresses the symbol body directly | | **Live Incremental Sync** | `cam sync` hashes file contents; `cam watch` keeps the graph updated on save | …

readme.markdown: DataSentry Find bad data before your users do. Automatic data-quality discovery, evidence-backed explanations, and safe reversible repair. Local-first. Deterministic by default. AI optional. Live demo · 30-second start · Use cases · FAQ · PyPI · Examples · MCP setup · Contribute > **中文导读**：DataSentry 会先自动发现数据质量问题，再给出样本、比例、置信度等证据。修复采用 `propose → preview → apply to a copy → verify → rollback` 的保守流程。检测与评分不依赖 LLM，AI 只作为可选辅助，数据可以完全留在本机。 ## Try it in 30 seconds Install the current PyPI release and run the zero-config product tour: ```bash pip install --upgrade datasentry-ai datasentry demo ``` `datasentry-demo` is also available as a direct console alias. The demo generates synthetic dirty data, runs the built-in detectors, exports JSON + HTML reports, applies one safe repair to a copy, re-scans the repaired copy, and prints a rollback command. It needs no dataset, cloud service, API key, or LLM. ```text synthetic dirty CSV ↓ 39 deterministic detectors ↓ evidence-backed issues + quality score ↓ preview → repaired copy ↓ re-scan → verify new/persistent issues ``` Prefer scanning your own data immediately? ```bash curl -L https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Jackxiaozhiren/datasentry/main/demo-data/orders.csv -o orders.csv datasentry scan orders.csv datasentry issues list --severity high ``` Or launch the interactive interfaces: ```bash datasentry # terminal UI datasentry-server # Web UI + REST API at http://localhost:8000/ui/ ``` ## Start with your problem | If you need to... | Start here | |---|---| | Find suspicious data before you know every rule | `datasentry scan data.csv` | | See the full discovery → repair → verify loop | `datasentry demo` | | Block severe data issues in CI | [`docs/GITHUB_ACTIONS.md`](docs/GITHUB_ACTIONS.md) | | Add quality gates to dbt / Airflow | [`examples/integrations/`](examples/integrations/) | | Inspect and repair issues without overwriting the source | [`Safe repair`](#safe-repair-not-blind-mutation) | | Give AI agents deterministic data-quality tools | [`docs/MCP.md`](docs/MCP.md) | The default path is intentionally low-commitment: **scan first, inspect evidence, then decide whether a finding deserves a permanent rule or a repair.** ## Why DataSentry exists Most data-quality tools are excellent once you already know the expectations, checks, or contracts you want to enforce. Real incidents often start one step earlier: **you do not yet know what is wrong.** DataSentry is built around the complete remediation loop: ```text Find → Explain → Fix safely → Verify ``` - **Find** — discover common quality problems without writing every rule first. - **Explain** — attach samples, affected counts/ratios, detector evidence, and confidence. - **Fix safely** — preview changes and apply repairs to a copy instead of mutating the source. - **Verify** — re-scan the repaired copy and surface persistent or newly introduced issues. DataSentry fits best when you are looking at data you do not fully trust yet, want evidence before codifying checks, or need a conservative remediation path. It complements expectation- and contract-driven tools rather than requiring you to replace them. ## What it catches automatically DataSentry ships with **39 deterministic detectors** covering common failure modes such as: - missing and placeholder values; - invalid emails, URLs, dates, and encodings; - duplicate identifiers and uniqueness violations; - inconsistent categories and cross-field contradictions; - foreign-key and referential-integrity problems; - numeric and statistical outliers; - schema, row-count, score, and issue-distribution drift. Every scan produces an evidence-backed issue list and a six-dimension quality score across completeness, validity, uniqueness, consistency, integrity, and timeliness. ## Safe repair, not blind mutation ```bash # inspect the highest-severity findings datasentry issues list --severity high # propose a repair without changing data datasentry repair propose --file orders.csv # preview the exact effect datasentry repair preview --file orders.csv # apply to a repaired copy; the original is not overwritten datasentry repair apply --file orders.csv # re-scan the repaired copy and detect regressions datasentry repair verify # inspect or undo the repair datasentry repair diff datasentry repair rollback ``` Repairs are fingerprinted, auditable, and reversible. AI-generated repair proposals remain human-approved state changes. ### Quality gates for CI ```bash datasentry scan orders.csv --fail-on high ``` For GitHub repositories, reuse DataSentry's maintained `workflow_call` gate instead of duplicating installation and exit-code handling: ```yaml jobs: datasentry: uses: Jackxiaozhiren/datasentry/.github/workflows/datasentry-quality-gate.yml@main with: path: data/orders.csv fail_on: high ``` See [`docs/GITHUB_ACTIONS.md`](docs/GITHUB_ACTIONS.md) for inputs, artifacts, security boundaries, and version-pinning guidance. Reports can be exported as JSON, Markdown, HTML, JUnit, and SARIF. The versioned, machine-readable [JSON report Schema](docs/REPORT_JSON_SCHEMA.md) is included for downstream validation. The GitHub Actions example fails the workflow on severe findings while still uploading an HTML report for review. ## Give AI agents deterministic data-quality tools DataSentry includes an MCP stdio server: ```bash datasentry mcp --project /path/to/project ``` MCP-capable clients can scan files, inspect evidence-backed issues, read quality scores and trends, compare drift, validate contracts, manage scheduled jobs, and call DataSentry tools without bypassing the same underlying safety rules used by the CLI and REST API. readme.markdown:
# Multi Calendar

Outlook.com, Microsoft 365, Google calendars: free time, events, invitations, booking pages, polls.

Multi Calendar is a remote MCP server run by Lumman Ltd. It puts every calendar account you connect - Outlook.com and Hotmail, Microsoft 365 and Google, several of each - behind one connector, so an AI client can find time free in all of them in one call, read and change events, answer invitations, and hand out booking links, booking pages and group polls. This repository holds what clients install: the manifests for Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI and Antigravity, three skills and their evals. The server itself is not in it.

## Before you start

You need a Lumman account with at least one calendar account connected - in the window your AI client opens when it first connects, or at https://lumman.co/mcp/account/multi-calendar. Sign in there with Google, Microsoft, a passkey or an emailed code. Outlook.com, Hotmail and Microsoft 365 calendars connect with Microsoft sign-in, Google calendars with Google sign-in. Each calendar account's permissions - seeing events, changing events, and inviting and replying - are set on the same page, and your time zone, working hours and other scheduling preferences on its Scheduling page, https://lumman.co/mcp/account/multi-calendar/scheduling.

## Add it to your client

### Claude

Open Multi Calendar in Claude's connectors directory, https://claude.ai/directory/connectors/lumman-multi-calendar, and press Connect. The listing connects at https://calendar.lumman.co/mcp.

### Claude Code

```
/plugin marketplace add lumman-lab/multi-calendar
/plugin install multi-calendar@multi-calendar
```

The plugin adds the connector at https://calendar.lumman.co/mcp and the three skills below. The first time a skill reaches the connector, Claude Code asks you to sign in; if it does not, run `/mcp` and choose the multi-calendar server.

### Cursor

Add the connector to `~/.cursor/mcp.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "multi-calendar": { "url": "https://calendar.lumman.co/mcp" }
  }
}
```

### VS Code

Run `MCP: Add Server`, choose `HTTP`, paste `https://calendar.lumman.co/mcp` and name it `multi-calendar`. Or add it to your user `mcp.json`:

```json
{
  "servers": {
    "multi-calendar": { "type": "http", "url": "https://calendar.lumman.co/mcp" }
  }
}
```

### Gemini CLI

```
gemini extensions install https://github.com/lumman-lab/multi-calendar
```

The extension adds the connector at https://calendar.lumman.co/mcp and the three skills below. Its first call opens Lumman's sign-in in your browser; `/mcp auth multi-calendar` opens it again.

### Antigravity

```
agy plugin install https://github.com/lumman-lab/multi-calendar
```

The plugin adds the connector at https://calendar.lumman.co/mcp and the three skills below, for the Antigravity CLI, app and IDE alike. To sign in, run `/mcp` in the CLI, open `multi-calendar_multi-calendar` and choose Authenticate, or in the app or IDE press Authenticate next to it under Agent settings, Customizations; approve on the Lumman page that opens, then paste the code Antigravity's page shows back into Antigravity.

### ChatGPT

This needs ChatGPT on the web, in a Business workspace where you are an admin or owner, or an Enterprise or Edu workspace whose role allows creating plugins with MCPs. On Pro it runs read tools alone; Plus and Free cannot add it.

1. Open chatgpt.com/plugins, press +, then Add custom MCP server.
2. Name it Multi Calendar, paste `https://calendar.lumman.co/mcp`, choose OAuth, tick the box and press Create as a plugin.
3. Install it. On the Lumman page, sign in, add a calendar if none is connected, and approve.
4. In a chat, type @ and choose Multi Calendar.

### Any other client

Add a remote MCP server at `https://calendar.lumman.co/mcp`: Streamable HTTP, OAuth 2.1 with dynamic client registration. No key or client id is needed.

## Signing in

The connector answers a client's first call with where to sign in. The client registers itself with Lumman's authorisation server and opens a Lumman page that names it: sign in, add a calendar if none is connected, and approve. Every client you approve is listed under Connected AI clients at https://lumman.co/mcp/account/multi-calendar, where its access can be taken back.

## Skills

Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI and Antigravity load three skills with the connector, and pick one by themselves when a request matches it. In Claude Code each is also a command, such as `/multi-calendar:week`.

- `free-time` - when you are free across every calendar, within your working hours, or when everyone in one of your circles is, with every calendar it could not read named. Books nothing.
- `meetings` - a meeting with guests shown to you as a draft, then made and its invitations sent only after you say yes to that draft.
- `week` - the week across every calendar, each meeting once, day by day, with clashes and unanswered invitations named. Changes nothing.

Examples:

- "When am I free for an hour on Thursday across all my calendars?"
- "Set up a 30-minute call with sam@example.com from my Outlook calendar on Thursday at 15:00."
- "What's on my calendars this week?"

name: OwnMemory
description: Encrypted memory for Claude, on a server you deploy to your own Cloudflare account.

readme.markdown:
OwnMemory lets Claude remember you across chats and devices, with the memories stored encrypted under a key only you hold, in storage you own.

Claude calls a remote MCP server running in your own Cloudflare account. The server encrypts each memory and stores it in a D1 database in that account (the one-click default) or in an `OwnMemory` folder in your Google Drive. It works in the official Claude apps on the web, iPhone and Android.

**Get started:** create a free Cloudflare account and connect GitHub to it first ([steps](docs/setup.md#one-click-setup)), then click the button above, choose a random owner code of 12+ characters, and open your server's address to follow its four setup steps. About 5 minutes, on a free Cloudflare account. Full guide, including Google Drive storage: [docs/setup.md](docs/setup.md).

**Status:** early (v0.2). Built and tested for Claude: on the web, iPhone and Android, and in Claude Code. Other MCP clients that support remote servers with OAuth should be able to connect, but are untested.

## How your memories stay yours

- **Your passphrase never leaves your browser.** When you connect Claude, the passphrase page turns it into a key that unlocks a random 256-bit memory key. Only the locked copy of that key is stored, in your storage (`keyinfo.json`).
- **Every memory is encrypted** (AES-256-GCM) before it is stored, in a file with a random name. Your storage provider and anyone with the files see only ciphertext.
- **The server keeps no key at rest.** The memory key and your Google token live only inside the OAuth grant, which is encrypted with Claude's access token. The MCP handler is stateless: nothing is written to Durable Objects or logs.
- **Hard rules in code.** Blocked categories, a pause switch, and a filter that refuses passwords, API keys and card numbers, whatever the AI decides.
- **Search by meaning, still private.** Embeddings come from Cloudflare Workers AI in your own account and are stored encrypted like the memories. Set the `SEMANTIC_SEARCH` secret to `off` to keep memory text away from it; search then uses keywords only.
- **See and fix what it remembers.** Your server's `/memories` page lets you browse, search, edit, add and delete memories, decrypted only in your browser.
- **No lock-in.** **Download all** on the memories page gives you every memory as Markdown, and [ownmemory.app/decrypt](https://ownmemory.app/decrypt) decrypts a downloaded copy in your browser, even without your server.

The one unavoidable exposure: the server and Anthropic see a memory's text while a save or search runs, because Claude sends plain text. Running the server yourself is the safeguard.

Who else could get at your memories, person by person, and how to keep them out: [docs/security-model.md](docs/security-model.md).

## Tools Claude gets

| Tool | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `load_core_memories` | Called at the start of a chat: returns the memory mode, any message for you, and (in OwnMemory-only mode) your profile, preferences and recent work |
| `search_memories` | Search by meaning and keywords, English, Chinese or mixed (finds "What do I like to drink?" without shared words) |
| `list_memories` | Most recent memories, optionally by category |
| `save_memory` | Saves one fact, after the hard rules allow it; points out facts already saved, even when worded differently |
| `import_memories` | Saves up to 50 facts at once, for example everything Claude's built-in memory knows |
| `update_memory` | Changes a fact, keeping the previous wording as dated history |
| `delete_memory` | Deletes a memory; it stays 30 days in D1, or in the Drive trash |
| `review_memories` | Finds memories with the same wording or meaning, to merge |
| `set_memory_mode` | Records how you use OwnMemory alongside Claude's memory: ramp-up, OwnMemory only, or keep both |

## Repository layout

| Path | What's there |
| --- | --- |
| `server/src/` | The Cloudflare Worker: OAuth and sign-in flow (`auth.ts`), passkey and authenticator sign-in on one-click servers (`gate.ts`, `factors.ts`), the memories page's API (`memories.ts`), MCP tools (`tools.ts`), storage backends D1 and Drive (`storage.ts`, `google.ts`), encrypted memory store (`store.ts`), memory format, search and duplicate checks (`format.ts`), memory modes and ramp-up (`settings.ts`), pages (`pages.ts`) |
| `server/public/unlock.js`, `home.js`, `memories.js`, `gate.js` | Scripts for the passphrase page, the setup wizard, the memories page and the passkey / authenticator sign-in step |
| `server/public/keys.js`, `memory-file.js`, `zip.js` | Encryption, the memory file format and the zip builder, shared by the browser, the Worker, the decrypt tool and `site/public/decrypt.html` (copies; `npm run sync-site`), so the format can't drift |
| `site/` | The ownmemory.app landing page and [the decrypt page](https://ownmemory.app/decrypt): static files, no data collected |
| `server/scripts/decrypt.mjs` | Local export to plain Markdown |
| `server/test/` | Unit tests (`npm test`) and a recall evaluation against real embeddings (`npm run eval`) |
| `docs/` | Setup guide, "Who can read your memories" and the key-flow diagram |
| `design/logo/` | Logo sources from the design canvas and PNG/SVG exports |

## Contributing, security and license

- Contributions are welcome; see [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md). Contributors sign a short [contributor license agreement](CLA.md).
- Found a security problem? Please report it privately: [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).
- Licensed under the [Apache License 2.0](LICENSE). "OwnMemory" and the OwnMemory logo are trademarks of the project and are not covered by the license; forks need a different name.

readme.markdown:
# codebase-memory-mcp: local code intelligence for AI agents via MCP

**Understand your repository, from source code to the systems around it.** codebase-memory-mcp is an MCP server that connects code, documentation, configuration, and infrastructure in a persistent local knowledge graph. Use it to find an unfamiliar feature, follow a call across services, trace a deployment back to its source, or assess which parts of a project a change could affect.

Give your coding agent structural context through [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/) (MCP), or query the graph directly from the CLI. **The MCP server is the core of the project.** Its optional visual companion, **CBM Lens, is in open beta (v0.0.1)**, with a source reader, architecture maps, the Galaxy graph, coverage diagnostics, architecture decisions, and local code chat.

The native C backend exposes **17 MCP tools**, parses [languages and file formats](#language-support) with vendored grammars, and adds [Hybrid LSP](#hybrid-lsp) type resolution for supported languages. The installer supports **45 automatic or conditional client integrations**, including client configuration, skills, agent profiles, and applicable hooks. Indexing and graph queries need no hosted service or API key. Focused graph queries can reduce repeated file reads and token use; see the [measured results](#performance).

[Quick start](#quick-start) · [Capabilities](#features) · [Documentation](#documentation-connected-to-code) · [Infrastructure](#infrastructure-and-deployment) · [Smart CI](#smart-ci-and-test-impact) · [Explore CBM Lens](#cbm-lens-beta-code-visualization-and-source-navigation) · [Agent setup](#agent-setup-skills-profiles-and-hooks) · [MCP tools](#mcp-tools)

> **Local processing:** Source analysis and graph storage run on your machine. CBM Lens can optionally download a model for browser AI after you enable it; inference stays on the device. The installer writes agent configuration for the clients you select. See [Security](#security) for release verification and [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) for reporting issues.

**See the graph with CBM Lens (open beta v0.0.1).** Folders become nested platforms, files and symbols become selectable blocks, and arrows show indexed relationships. The recording opens `src/foundation` in the map of this repository, selects `arena.c` and opens its source. Height can show source size; hotspot gravity reflects static fan-in. [Still image](docs/images/lens-architecture.png).

  

**Galaxy.** Explore the code knowledge graph in 3D. The recording follows the outgoing relationships of `cbm_arena_alloc` one layer further, switches to the hierarchy and shows the two-hop call path to `cbm_alloc`. Edge pulses show relationship direction; they do not represent live execution. [Still: two dependency layers around `cbm_max_file_bytes`](docs/images/lens-galaxy.jpg).

  

**Explore.** Browse files in an IDE-style workspace, read syntax-highlighted source in Monaco, and keep the code graph alongside it. File impact shows what depends on the open file, and Code details shows the callers and calls of the symbol under the caret. Select code to [ask the local chat about it](#chat-with-your-codebase-locally).

<details>
<summary>More views: system structure and behavior</summary>

System structure groups symbols into components and lets you inspect their dependencies.

Behavior shows possible calls from a selected operation and the source evidence behind them.

</details>

The high-resolution GIFs show CBM Lens Beta on 20 October 2026; the still images were captured on 12–13 October. All show public source from this repository. See [capture details](docs/images/README.md) for each capture's build, indexed scope and recording setup.

## Why codebase-memory-mcp

- **Find the right code with context**: combine symbol, text, and semantic search with callers, dependencies, source snippets, and file outlines. Targeted queries and compact, paged results can reduce token use and repeated file reads; see [Performance](#performance) for scoped measurements.
- **Connect documentation to implementation**: index document sections, PDF text pages, architecture decisions, and supported references into code. Find the explanation alongside the symbol.
- **Follow the system beyond source files**: trace supported relationships through Docker, Kubernetes, Helm, Kustomize, Terraform/OpenTofu, Terragrunt, Ansible, scripts, Make, and CI configuration.
- **Understand a change before running it**: inspect affected symbols, compare indexed snapshots, and find related tests. [Experimental Smart CI](#smart-ci-and-test-impact) combines static relationships and per-test coverage for supported C/C++ test harnesses, falling back to broader runs when evidence is insufficient.
- **Explore visually with CBM Lens Beta**: read source, follow call paths, inspect architecture and coverage gaps, manage architecture decisions, and ask a local model about selected code.
- **Equip your coding agents**: `install` sets up supported client configuration, durable guidance, skills, Scout/Verify/Auditor profiles, and applicable context hooks. Support varies by client; see the [integration matrix](#multi-agent-support).
- **Keep context local and reusable**: indexes persist between sessions, eligible active MCP sessions can keep them synchronized, and optional graph artifacts let a team share a baseline.
- **Run a native tool on your machine**: standard releases include CBM Lens for macOS, Linux, and Windows. The native runtime needs no Docker or language runtime; parser grammars are included.

## Quick Start

**Install the latest release** (macOS / Linux):
```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DeusData/codebase-memory-mcp/main/install.sh | bash
```

The standard native release includes CBM Lens. Start it after installation with `codebase-memory-mcp daemon start --open --port=9749`. The [Nix packages](#nix-flake) and [source builds](#build-from-source) a

readme.markdown:
ZenBrain The neuroscience-inspired memory system for AI agents. 7 memory layers and a library of 20 neuroscience-inspired algorithm modules: FSRS, Hebbian learning, sleep replay, emotional tagging, plus 10 advanced research modules (vmPFC-FSRS, two-factor Hebbian, simulation-selection sleep, Fiedler-value KG health, IB budget, Hopfield STM, ...).Pure TypeScript. No third-party dependencies in algorithms and core. 945 tests. Extracted from a production AI platform. Status: pre-1.0, semver — the public API can still change before 1.0. 945 tests green in CI: 933 on each of Node 22, 24 and 26, and 12 more against PostgreSQL with pgvector · the current version of every package published to npm with build provenance · every change recorded in the CHANGELOG · issues and pull requests are answered; replications and counter-results are especially welcome. Self-hosted: the library makes no network calls of its own. Memory lives in SQLite or PostgreSQL that you operate; an embedding model or an LLM is optional and your choice. --- ▶ Try the live playground in your browser — runs this published code, no install required.
📄 Paper & Citation — ZenBrain: A Neuroscience-Inspired 7-Layer Memory Architecture for Autonomous AI Systems - **arXiv preprint** (cs.AI): [arxiv.org/abs/2604.23878](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.23878) - **Open-access archive** (Zenodo / CERN): [doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19353663](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19353663) - **ORCID**: [0009-0001-1793-012X](https://orcid.org/0009-0001-1793-012X) - **License**: CC BY 4.0 (paper) · Apache-2.0 (code) ```bibtex @misc{bering2026zenbrain, title = {ZenBrain: A Neuroscience-Inspired 7-Layer Memory Architecture for Autonomous AI Systems}, author = {Bering, Alexander}, year = {2026}, eprint = {2604.23878}, archivePrefix = {arXiv}, primaryClass = {cs.AI}, doi = {10.5281/zenodo.19353663}, url = {https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.23878} } ``` Feedback, replications, and counter-results are explicitly welcome — please open an issue or reach out via [research@zensation.ai](mailto:research@zensation.ai).
> **Your AI forgets everything after every conversation.** ZenBrain gives it a memory that lasts across sessions, split into layers the way human memory is, and ships the mechanisms memory research describes (spaced repetition, emotional tagging, Hebbian strengthening, forgetting curves, sleep replay) as tested functions. Which of them run on their own and which you call yourself is in [one table](#what-runs-on-its-own-and-what-you-call-yourself). > **Architecture vs. this package.** ZenBrain's architecture is **15 neuroscience-inspired mechanisms — 9 foundational algorithms + 6 Predictive Memory Architecture (PMA) components** ([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.23878)). The six PMA components are proprietary: they ran in the ZenAI production system and are not in these packages, which contain the hooks they plug into. **This open-source package ships the algorithm library: 10 core algorithms + 10 advanced research modules (20 modules), zero-dependency.** --- ## Benchmark: LongMemEval-500 On LongMemEval-500, **three of nine head-to-head comparisons hold** against Letta, Mem0 and A-Mem — all three against A-Mem, the remaining six are ties, none lost. The figures above were not measured with this package: per the correction notice, the measured arm is a Python port of a test-harness class, not an import of the packages. The paper prints where ZenBrain loses as well: on LoCoMo, substring-based aggregate F1 favours lexical retrieval (BM25) by metric design, and we do not contest that. The advantage is most pronounced in the judge-graded comparisons and on cross-session reasoning. **The mechanism comparison further down re-runs from this repository in under a minute** — `bash scripts/compare-mechanisms.sh`, no API keys; it needs git, Node and network access to clone the three compared repositories at the pinned commits. It prints a positive and a negative control before the result, so the instrument can be checked before its output is trusted. **The mechanism ablation behind paper Tables 7–9 also runs from here:** `cd backend && npm run experiments`, and CI compares every point estimate with the published ones. [English](README.en.md) · **Español**

# MCP Memory — Memoria local para agentes IA vía MCP

> **Lleva la memoria de tu agente IA a cualquier máquina.**
> Servidor MCP open source que da memoria persistente con búsqueda léxica (BM25) a Claude Desktop, Claude Code, OpenCode, Cursor, Continue y cualquier cliente compatible con [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io). SQLite + FTS5, **cero infra externa, 100% en tu hardware**.

**Tags:** `mcp-server` · `ai-agents` · `sqlite` · `fts5` · `bm25` · `claude-code` · `cursor` · `opencode` · `lexical-search` · `agent-memory` · `local-first` · `self-hosted`

  

<sub>El agente guarda algo en una sesión y lo recuerda en otra — mismo archivo SQLite, proceso nuevo. Sin nube, sin vectores, sin servicios extra.</sub>

---

## 💡 Por qué existe

Los agentes IA olvidan todo entre conversaciones. Las soluciones existentes son cloud-only, multi-tenant pesado, o están atadas a un único cliente. **MCP Memory** resuelve esto con tres ideas simples:

1. **Tu memoria, tu máquina.** Un solo archivo SQLite local. Cero datos en la nube, cero servicios externos que levantar.
2. **Conectas una vez, funciona en todos lados.** Es un servidor MCP estándar — cualquier cliente que hable MCP lo usa sin custom code.
3. **Cero overhead.** `pip install` y tienes 9 tools listas para tu agente en segundos — sin Docker, sin modelos que descargar.

---

## ⚡ Quickstart

Hay dos formas de correrlo. Elige una:

| Modo | Cuándo | Cómo arranca |
|------|--------|--------------|
| **stdio** | Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor… (lo más simple) | El cliente lanza el proceso él solo. No hay server de fondo ni puerto. |
| **HTTP** | Varios clientes contra un mismo server, Docker, clientes web | Lo arrancas tú y queda escuchando en `http://localhost:8765/mcp`. |

### Opción A — stdio (sin dejar nada corriendo)

Con [`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) **0.13.4 o superior** instalado no hace falta clonar (las versiones anteriores confían en una CA comprometida, ver [`SECURITY.md`](SECURITY.md#cadena-de-suministro-incidente-emudhra)): el cliente descarga y lanza el server en cada sesión. Para Claude Code:

```bash
claude mcp add -s user mcp-memory -- uvx --from "git+https://github.com/GermaniU/mcp-memory#subdirectory=server" mcp-memory --stdio
```

Para Claude Desktop, Cursor y el resto, la config JSON está en [`docs/CLIENTS.md`](docs/CLIENTS.md#modo-stdio-recomendado). Todos los procesos comparten el mismo archivo SQLite (`DB_PATH`), así que la memoria es la misma en todos tus clientes.

### Opción B — HTTP (server de fondo)

```bash
git clone https://github.com/GermaniU/mcp-memory.git
cd mcp-memory/server
pip install -e .
mcp-memory
```

> Alternativa sin instalar en tu entorno global: `uvx --from . mcp-memory` (corriendo dentro de `server/`).

No hay pre-requisitos: nada que levantar, nada que descargar. Al arrancar, el server crea el archivo SQLite (`DB_PATH`, default `~/.agent-memory/memory.db`) y su schema (tabla `memories` + índice FTS5) si no existen.

Endpoint MCP: `http://localhost:8765/mcp`. Pégalo en la config de tu cliente (ver [`docs/CLIENTS.md`](docs/CLIENTS.md) — Claude Code, OpenCode, Cursor, Continue).

> `mcp-memory --stdio` (o `MCP_TRANSPORT=stdio`) arranca el modo stdio con la instalación local.

### 🔍 Diagnóstico y Chequeo de Salud

Verifica que tu Python tiene FTS5 compilado y que `DB_PATH` es accesible al instante:

```bash
mcp-memory check
```

`mcp-memory --help` lista los comandos y variables de entorno; `mcp-memory --version` imprime la versión instalada.

---

## 🛠 Tools MCP expuestas

| Tool             | Tipo | Para qué |
|------------------|------|----------|
| `memory_save`    | ✏️ escritura | Guardar texto + tags + metadata. |
| `memory_search`  | 👁 lectura | Búsqueda léxica (BM25 vía SQLite FTS5) con filtro por namespace. |
| `memory_update`  | ⚠️ destructiva | Cambiar contenido/tags/metadata por id. Re-sincroniza el índice FTS5 si cambia el contenido. Rechaza `content` vacío. |
| `memory_delete`  | ⚠️ destructiva | Borrar por id. |
| `memory_list`    | 👁 lectura | Paginado por namespace. |
| `memory_recent`  | 👁 lectura | Las últimas N por `updated_at`. |
| `memory_stats`   | 👁 lectura | Conteo, namespaces, oldest/newest. |
| `memory_export`  | 👁 lectura | Exporta todas las memorias (o las de un namespace) como JSONL. Devuelve `count` y el string `jsonl`. |
| `memory_import`  | ✏️ escritura | Importa un string JSONL producido por `memory_export`. Salta colisiones de id silenciosamente. Acepta `namespace_override` opcional. |

El **Tipo** se publica como [anotaciones MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/server/tools#tool-annotations) (`readOnlyHint`, `destructiveHint`): los clientes que las soportan pueden auto-aprobar las lecturas y pedir confirmación antes de modificar o borrar. Al conectarse, el server también envía `instructions` al agente (cuándo buscar, cuándo guardar, cómo formular queries léxicas).

Schemas + ejemplos de invocación en [`docs/CLIENTS.md`](docs/CLIENTS.md).

---

## 🎯 Alcance actual

MCP Memory es deliberadamente pequeño. Hace **una cosa bien: memoria léxica de texto plano**. No es un sistema de RAG completo, no es un knowledge base, no es un grafo.

### Lo que SÍ hace
- ✅ Almacena y recupera **texto puro** en SQLite.
- ✅ Búsqueda léxica (BM25/FTS5) con filtro por `namespace`.
- ✅ Tags + metadata libres en cada entrada.
- ✅ 9 tools MCP estándar para cualquier agente compatible.
- ✅ Persistencia en disco (un único archivo `.db`), backup = copiar el archivo.

### Lo que NO hace (todavía)
- ❌ **No hace búsqueda semántica.** Es léxica (BM25): coincide términos, no significado — sinónimos o paráfrasis sin overlap de vocabulario no matchean.
- ❌ **No soporta imágenes ni gráficas.** Solo texto.
- ❌ **No soporta PDFs ni archivos binarios** — extrae el texto antes de guardarlo.
- ❌ **No es multi-tenant.** Una persona, una máquina, una memoria (con namespaces para separar contextos).
- ❌ **No ti

readme.markdown:
# MemoryComb

**One memory. Every AI. Your whole team.**

MemoryComb is a memory library that lives on your computer. Claude, ChatGPT and your other AIs all read and write the same memory, so you stop re-explaining yourself every time you switch AIs. Every read has a receipt, and an AI Scorecard shows which AI's facts turned out wrong.

**Built to be trusted:** every memory is checked for hidden instructions before any AI reads it, your AIs can fact-check each other (you settle any disagreement), and your memory stays on your computer with encrypted backups to your own iCloud Drive or OneDrive.

This page has the downloads only. MemoryComb is in early testing on **Mac and Windows** (Windows is newer: tell us what breaks).

## Install (pick one)

By installing MemoryComb you agree to the [License](LICENSE.md). Please also read the [Privacy Policy](PRIVACY.md).

### If you use the Claude app (easiest)
1. Download **memorycomb-*.mcpb** from the [latest release](../../releases/latest).
2. Double-click it. Claude opens its install screen; click **Install**.
   Claude shows a red "not verified" warning for every extension that isn't in its directory yet. What MemoryComb touches: only its own memory folder on your computer (`~/.memorycomb`) and an encrypted daily backup in your iCloud Drive (Mac) or OneDrive (Windows).
3. Start a new chat and ask: **"What's in my MemoryComb?"**

### Mac: Terminal (Claude Code, ChatGPT and everything else)
```bash
curl -fsSL https://github.com/BryceBlackRoot/memorycomb/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
```

### Windows: PowerShell (early test)
```powershell
irm https://github.com/BryceBlackRoot/memorycomb/releases/latest/download/install.ps1 | iex
```
It installs MemoryComb for your user only (no admin password), starts it at login, and opens the dashboard's **Get started** page.

## After installing
Your dashboard is at **http://127.0.0.1:8765** (it only opens on your own computer). From there:
- **Get started**: tap the AI you're connecting.
- **Import**: bring in what ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or Grok already know about you.
- **Team**: share one memory with the people you work with (test version: runs while your computer is on).

## Privacy
Your memory never leaves your computer unless you switch on sharing (for ChatGPT or teammates). MemoryComb goes online only to check for a newer version once a day (it asks for the version number, nothing else) and for sharing you switch on.

## Free
MemoryComb is free. Everything is included: unlimited memories, every AI, every trust feature, and team sharing. No trial, nothing to buy, and nothing is ever deleted. Team sharing runs from the computer of whoever starts the shared project, so teammates can reach it while that computer is on.

## Uninstall
```bash
~/.local/bin/memorycomb uninstall
```
On Windows: `memorycomb uninstall` in PowerShell.
This removes the app and its login item but **keeps your memory** in `~/.memorycomb`. In the Claude app, remove the extension under Settings › Extensions.

## Feedback
Found a problem or have an idea? Open an issue on this page.

## Legal
[License](LICENSE.md) · [Privacy Policy](PRIVACY.md) · [Third-party notices](THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md)

MemoryComb is early test software provided as is. Memories and AI answers can be wrong: check anything important yourself. Nothing in MemoryComb is professional advice.

readme.markdown:
# GitHub Organization Signal Scanner MCP Server

An MCP server that resolves a company domain to its GitHub organization with repo, language and activity signals. It wraps the Mamba Labs GitHub Organization Signal Scanner actor on Apify and returns a Clay-ready flat JSON row to any MCP client.

## What's Inside

- [What it does](#what-it-does)
- [Quick start](#quick-start)
- [Prerequisites](#prerequisites)
- [Example prompts](#example-prompts)
- [Inputs](#inputs)
- [Output](#output)
- [Example output](#example-output)
- [Features](#features)
- [Full actor documentation](#full-actor-documentation)
- [Mamba Labs GTM Suite](#mamba-labs-gtm-suite)
- [License](#license)

## What it does

Give it a company domain and it finds that company's GitHub organization and returns repository count, followers, creation date, top languages, total stars, the most recent push, how many repositories are actively worked on, and whether the company ships a public SDK. One flat row per company, read through GitHub's own documented REST API.

Forks and archived repositories are excluded from the language and star derivations, and the exclusion is counted on the row. A rate limited request reports `not_extractable` and never a zero, because a zero is a number a buyer would filter on. A login that resolves to a personal user account rather than an organization is reported as `identity_mismatch`. It reads organization and repository metadata only: it does not clone repositories, read source, scan for secrets or assess code quality.

All of the scanning runs on Apify. This package is a thin client that calls the actor and hands back the result unchanged.

## Quick start

You need Node.js 18 or newer and an Apify account with an API token.

Add this to your Claude Desktop config:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "mamba-github-organization-signal-scanner": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@mambalabsdev/mcp-github-organization-signal-scanner"],
      "env": {
        "APIFY_TOKEN": "your-apify-token"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Get your token at https://console.apify.com/account/integrations, paste it in, and restart Claude Desktop. The `scan_github_organization_signals` tool will be available.

## Prerequisites

- Node.js 18 or newer
- An Apify account with an API token
- Optional: your own GitHub personal access token, free to create at github.com/settings/tokens with no scopes at all for public data, if you want to scan more than a handful of companies

## Example prompts

- "Find the GitHub organization for stripe.com and summarize its activity."
- "Scan the GitHub org `vercel` and tell me its top languages and total stars."
- "Does figma.com ship a public SDK? Check its GitHub organization."
- "Scan notion.so's GitHub org, counting a repo as active if it was pushed in the last 30 days."

## Inputs

- `company_domain` (optional): bare company domain, for example `stripe.com`. This is the lookup key and the join key for every other actor in the fleet.
- `company_name` (optional but strongly recommended): what the identity gate checks a discovered record against, so supplying it is the cheapest way to reduce wrong matches.
- `github_org` (optional): if you already know the organization login, for example `stripe`, put it here and the tool skips discovery entirely and goes straight to the API, which is faster and spends fewer rate limited requests.
- `includeRepoDetail` (optional): when true (the default) the organization repositories are read and the language, star, activity and SDK signals are derived from them. Set false to return the organization record only, which is one request instead of several and is friendlier to the unauthenticated rate limit.
- `includeContributorEstimate` (optional): when true one extra request reads the contributor count of the organization's most starred repository, as a floor on the size of its public engineering surface. False by default, because one extra request per company is real money against a 60 per hour unauthenticated budget.
- `activeWindowDays` (optional): how recently a repository must have been pushed to count as active. One of `30`, `90`, `180` or `365`, with 90 the default. This changes what active means on the row.
- `repoPageBudget` (optional): how many pages of 100 repositories to read for a large organization. One of `1`, `2`, `3` or `5`. This is a cost and completeness dial, not a change of answer: the row always reports how many repositories were sampled and whether the sample is complete.
- `githubToken` (optional): your own GitHub personal access token, free to create with no scopes at all for public data. Without it the tool runs at GitHub's 60 requests per hour, which is enough for a handful of companies and not enough for a list. With it the limit is 5,000 per hour.
- `skipCache` (optional): when false (the default) a successful lookup is cached for seven days and reused. Set true to force a fresh fetch.
- `max_charge_usd` (optional): a cost cap in USD for this run. The actor stops before an item that could take its charges past this amount. Omit it to rely on the maximum cost per run set in Apify.

## Output

The tool returns the actor's flat JSON row for the company, with 32 snake_case fields and no nested objects. `github_discovery` says how the organization was found, `github_rejected_candidate` records a candidate the identity gate turned away, `repos_sampled` and `repos_complete` say how much of the organization was read, and `repos_excluded` counts the forks and archived repositories left out. See the Apify Store page for the full output schema.

## Example output

```json
{
  "degraded": false,
  "degradation_reason": null,
  "company_domain": "stripe.com",
  "company_name": "Stripe",
  "github_org": "stripe",
  "github_url": "https://github.com/stripe",
  "github_discovery": "homepage_link",
  "github_rejected_candidate": null,
  "github_account_type": "Organization",
  "public_repos": 98,
  "followers": 3469,
  "org_created_at": "2011-0

…

readme.markdown:
# Korely Memory

Memory for AI agents that knows what is still true.

Korely stores what your agent learns as **typed facts with a validity window**. When something changes, the old fact is superseded instead of overwritten. Your agent reads the current truth, and you can still ask what was true on any past date.

```python
import time
from korely_memory import Korely

korely = Korely()  # reads KORELY_API_KEY from the environment

korely.add("Maria is on the Pro plan, billed yearly.", user_id="maria")
korely.add("Maria downgraded to Free.", user_id="maria")

time.sleep(10)  # facts are extracted server-side; see "Writes settle asynchronously"

ctx = korely.get_context(query="what plan is Maria on?", user_id="maria")
print(ctx.context)
# ## Known facts
# - Maria downgraded_to Free (since 2026-09-08)
# - Maria billing_frequency yearly (since 2026-09-08)
#
# Pro is gone from the current facts. It was superseded, not deleted.
```

The exact predicate is chosen by the extractor, so `downgraded_to` here might be
`subscribes_to` or `plan` on your run. What is guaranteed is the behaviour: the
old value leaves the current set, and stays retrievable with its `invalid_at`.

Nothing was deleted. The Pro fact is still there, carrying `invalid_at` and a pointer to what replaced it:

```python
korely.get_facts(user_id="maria", include_invalidated=True)
# Maria downgraded_to Free    valid_from=... invalid_at=None
# Maria plan Pro              valid_from=... invalid_at=2026-09-08T08:31:09Z
```

## Time travel over real dates

Pass `timestamp` when the event happened in the past, and facts inherit it as
`valid_from`. Then `as_of` answers over the world's timeline, not your ingestion
order:

```python
korely.add("Franco signed up on the Pro plan.", user_id="franco", timestamp="2026-01-15")
korely.add("Franco downgraded to Free.",        user_id="franco", timestamp="2026-06-20")

korely.get_facts(user_id="franco", as_of="2026-03-01")   # subscribes_to -> Pro plan
korely.get_facts(user_id="franco", as_of="2026-08-01")   # subscribes_to -> Free
korely.get_facts(user_id="franco")                       # subscribes_to -> Free
```

Without `timestamp` every fact starts being true the moment you write it, so
`as_of` on an earlier date returns nothing. That is correct, and usually not
what you want when you are importing history.

`as_of` answers what was true on a date, as the store knows it today.
`known_as_of` (Korely Agent 0.1.26) answers the other question: what the store
knew on that date. They differ when a change is told late. An agent learns on
5 October that a customer moved on 1 September:

```python
korely.get_facts(user_id="maria", as_of="2026-09-20")        # lives_in -> Turin
korely.get_facts(user_id="maria", known_as_of="2026-09-20")  # lives_in -> Milan
```

On 20 September the move had happened, and the store did not know it yet.
`known_as_of` is on `get_facts`, `get_profile` and `get_context`, which rebuilds
the block as the store could have built it then: what an agent could have
known when it decided. Each fact carries `closed_known_at`, when the store
learned it had ended.

## Writes settle asynchronously

`add()` returns as soon as the memory is stored, then extraction runs server-side. That means:

| Call | Available |
|---|---|
| `search()` over raw memories | immediately |
| `get_facts()` and `get_context()` typed facts | after a few seconds |

The `time.sleep(10)` above exists only so the snippet works when you paste it. **You do not need it in production**: an agent writes at the end of one turn and reads at the start of the next, and by then the facts are there.

If you do need to know exactly when, ask instead of guessing. Every memory carries a `status` of `processing`, `ready`, or `error`, and `events()` reports what is still in flight:

```python
page = korely.events()
page.processing  # 0
page.events[0]   # MemoryEvent(memory_id='mem_...', status='ready', ...)
```

`processing == 0` means none of your project's writes (in the `user_id` scope, if you pass one) is still being extracted, however many there are, so a script can wait on that one number instead of walking every id. After a `batch()` import, wait for `batch_status()` to finish first: memories the job has not stored yet are not counted.

Polling is the only signal: no webhook fires when extraction finishes. The webhook events are `memory.created`, `fact.invalidated` and `quota.warning`.

## Install

```bash
pip install korely-memory      # Python, plus the `korely` CLI
npm install korely-memory      # Node / TypeScript
```

Both clients have **zero runtime dependencies**.

For LangGraph, the optional `pip install 'korely-memory[langgraph]'` adds a store, memory tools and a context helper: see [python/README.md](python/README.md#langgraph).

## Get a key

# MySQL AIops

> **Disclaimer**: Community-maintained open-source project. **Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Oracle Corporation or the MariaDB Foundation.** "MySQL" is a trademark of Oracle Corporation; "MariaDB" is a trademark of MariaDB plc; all product/trademark names belong to their respective owners. MIT licensed.

Governed AI-ops for **MySQL 8.x and MariaDB 10.6+ DBA operations** — connecting
to a server with **PyMySQL** and reading `information_schema` /
`performance_schema` — with a **built-in governance harness**: unified audit
log, token/runaway budget guard, undo-token recording, and descriptive
risk-tier labels. The server **flavor** (mysql vs mariadb) is
detected from `version()` and flavor-dependent statements branch automatically
(`SHOW REPLICA STATUS` vs `SHOW SLAVE STATUS`).

## What it does

Four flagship signature analyses, plus the guarded reads and writes around them:

- **Slow-query RCA** — take the worst `events_statements_summary_by_digest`
  entry (plus an optional `EXPLAIN FORMAT=JSON` plan) and map its numbers —
  no-index share (`SUM_NO_INDEX_USED`), lock-time share, rows-examined/sent
  ratio, tmp-disk spill, call count, plan access types — to a cited cause and a
  concrete action. Every finding carries its measured number, not a black-box
  verdict.
- **InnoDB lock-wait & deadlock chain RCA** — build the wait-for tree from
  `performance_schema.data_lock_waits` (MariaDB:
  `information_schema.innodb_lock_waits`), name the **root blocker** (blocks
  others, waits on none), and parse the **last deadlock** out of
  `SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS`.
- **Replication lag RCA** — map the replica's IO/SQL thread state,
  `Seconds_Behind_Source` and error fields to a cited cause + action
  (stopped IO thread, failed applier statement, lagging applier, intentional
  `SQL_Delay`).
- **Table fragmentation analysis** — rank tables by reclaimable `data_free`
  from `information_schema.tables` into cited `OPTIMIZE TABLE` candidates.

## What works

- **CLI** (`mysql-aiops ...`): `init`, `overview`, `server`, `activity`, `query`, `index`, `table`, `repl`, `analyze`, `remediate`, `secret`, `doctor`, `mcp`.
- **MCP server** (`mysql-aiops mcp` or `mysql-aiops-mcp`): **35 tools** (26 read, 9 write), every one wrapped with the bundled `@governed_tool` harness.
- **Encrypted credentials**: the account password lives in an encrypted store `~/.mysql-aiops/secrets.enc` (Fernet + scrypt) — **never plaintext on disk**. Unlock with a master password from `MYSQL_AIOPS_MASTER_PASSWORD` (MCP/CI) or an interactive prompt (CLI).
- **Reversibility**: mutating writes fetch the **real before-state first** and record a faithful inverse — `create_index`↔`drop_index`; `drop_index` captures the index definition out of `SHOW CREATE TABLE` so undo recreates it exactly; `set_global_variable` captures the prior value from `SHOW GLOBAL VARIABLES` so undo sets it back. Irreversible ops (`kill_session`, `kill_query`, `optimize_table`, `analyze_table`, `reset_query_stats`) record prior state for audit but declare no undo.
- **Safety**: every state-changing CLI op supports `--dry-run` and requires double confirmation; every write MCP tool takes a `dry_run` preview. All identifiers that cannot be parameterised (schema/table/index/column/variable names) are validated against a strict charset and backtick-quoted; all values are bound query parameters.

## What this tool does, and does not, decide

It delivers MySQL / MariaDB DBA operations — reads and writes — accurately and
efficiently, and records every one of them. It does **not** decide whether a write is
allowed to happen. That is the agent's judgement, or the permission of the account you
connect it with: point it at a MySQL/MariaDB account granted only SELECT / PROCESS /
REPLICATION CLIENT and no write privileges (no INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/DDL), and the
writes fail at the server — the place that actually owns the permission.

So there is no read-only switch, no policy file, no approval gate to configure. The one
thing the tool guarantees is that nothing is silent: **every call, over MCP and over the
CLI alike, lands an audit row** in `~/.mysql-aiops/audit.db`, and destructive writes still
capture their before-state and record an inverse where one exists.

> Each tool declares a `risk_level`, carried into the audit row as a descriptive tier
> (none/confirm/review) — so a reviewer can see at a glance that a row was a high-risk delete. It
> is a label, not a gate.

[agent-guardrails.md](skills/mysql-aiops/references/agent-guardrails.md) — it lists
