# Browser MCP by [Agent360](https://agent360.dk)

**The browser tool that can stop and ask you.** A 2FA code, a CAPTCHA, a choice only you can
make: it asks on your own screen, then carries on in the same signed-in Chrome.

It drives the Chrome you are already signed into: no login step to fail, no API key to wire
up, no fresh profile that is a stranger to every account you have. Up to 20 agents at once, each
in its own colour-coded tab group. 40 tools, MIT, runs on your machine.

→ **[What it can and cannot get past](https://browsermcp.dev/docs/capability-matrix/)** - every
wall, marked *measured*, *by design*, *not yet*, or *won't*. Including the ones we have not fixed.

▶ **[Watch the 15-second film →](https://browsermcp.dev/film.mp4)**

Browser MCP gives Claude Code (and MCP clients that run local servers, such as Cursor and VS Code agent mode) control of your actual Chrome: your cookies, your sessions, your 2FA. So it works on CAPTCHA, 2FA and anti-bot sites where Playwright and Puppeteer get blocked - because it's *you* browsing.

The killer move: it hits a login wall, opens your Gmail, reads the verification code, and continues the sign-in. There is no email API to set up. Operate platforms with no API, QA your own web app end-to-end, or work dashboards, LinkedIn and Reddit at human pace - with you approving the sensitive steps.

40 tools. Auto-clicks the reCAPTCHA v2 checkbox, with a human fallback for the rest. Multi-session color-coded tab groups. **MIT, free, and it runs on your machine - no account, no telemetry, nothing sent to us.**

## The whole thing, in four steps

**Rather not do it by hand?** Paste this to your AI assistant - Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, VS Code, Windsurf, Cline - and it sets itself up:

> Set up Browser MCP for me. Read https://browsermcp.dev/llms-install.md and follow it for whichever AI client you are running in. One step only I can do - tell me which one, and wait for me. When I confirm, call `browser_list_tabs` to prove both halves are talking.
>
> If you cannot open URLs: `npx @agent360/browser-mcp install`

It reads the same guide the four steps below spell out by hand. One step stays yours either way: Chrome will not let an extension install itself, so you load it once.

**1 - Install the Chrome extension.** One click from the [Chrome Web Store](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/agent360-browser-mcp/jdehgalffmffhfhmmhaokfbfnafnmgcl); Chrome keeps it updated. No store? See the unpacked install below.

**2 - Add the MCP server.** Paste this in a terminal. Required - the extension does nothing on its own:

```bash
claude mcp add --scope user browser-mcp -- npx @agent360/browser-mcp@latest
```

**3 - Restart Claude Code.** That is what starts the server. The extension shows no badge until step 4 - the server only takes a port the first time your agent actually uses the browser. A green badge with the number of connected agents appears then; nothing on the icon before that is normal. (The icon itself never changes colour - it is the badge that turns green.)

**4 - Say this, to check it worked.** Paste it to Claude Code:

> Open example.com and take a screenshot.

You get an image back instead of *"I don't have browser access"*. **That's it - you're running.** → [What else to say](#youre-in-now-what)

Using Cursor, VS Code, Codex or Windsurf? Same server, that client's own config - the prompt at the top handles it, or see [browsermcp.dev/docs](https://browsermcp.dev/docs/install-cursor/). Everything below is the long version.

## The long version - install, step by step

> **Browser MCP is two halves and you need both:** a **Chrome extension** (drives the browser) and a **local MCP server** (what your agent actually talks to). Installing only the extension - e.g. straight from the Chrome Web Store - leaves it stuck on *"Not connected"*, because there is no server for it to reach. Chrome cannot install the server, and npm cannot install the extension. Hence two steps.

### Step 1: Register the MCP server with Claude Code

```bash
claude mcp add --scope user browser-mcp -- npx @agent360/browser-mcp@latest
```

That is Claude Code's own MCP command, so the entry lands in the config Claude Code actually reads. `--scope user` makes it available in every project.

Want the extension files on disk for the unpacked install in Step 2? Also run:

```bash
npx @agent360/browser-mcp install
```

It copies the extension to `~/.browser-mcp/extension/` and **prints that path in the terminal - copy it.** (It also registers the server with Claude Code, Codex, VS Code and Cursor if it finds them.)

### Step 2: Load the extension in Chrome

> Chrome won't let extensions install themselves from npm - you load it manually one time. To **update** later, re-run the install command and reload it (see [Keeping it updated](#keeping-it-updated)). Prefer the [Chrome Web Store](#chrome-web-store-no-developer-mode-auto-updating-extension) install if you'd rather have the extension auto-update.

1. **Open Chrome** and type `chrome://extensions` in the address bar
2. **Toggle "Developer mode"** ON (top right corner)
3. **Click "Load unpacked"** (top left, next to "Pack extension")
4. **Navigate to `~/.browser-mcp/extension/`** and click "Select"
   - On Mac: Press `Cmd+Shift+G` in the file picker, paste `~/.browser-mcp/extension/`, press Enter
   - On Windows: Paste `%USERPROFILE%\.browser-mcp\extension\` in the address bar (Windows is not yet verified: our automated tests do not pass there)
   - On Linux: Type `~/.browser-mcp/extension/` in the path field
5. **Restart Claude Code** so it picks up the new MCP server

That's it. The Browser MCP icon will appear in your toolbar, and 40 browser tools are now available in Claude Code.

If you don't want to use npm, download the extension directly:

# FIDE Laws of Chess on Arxo

**Explore a chess arbiter's decision through a pinned model, explicit facts and an inspectable answer.** Ten retained fictional cases cover illegal moves, flag fall, rapid/blitz exceptions, recording and arbiter judgment.

**Node.js 20+ · ESM · canon package 0.1.0 · model 0.1.1 · FIDE edition effective 1 January 2023**

[Start in Node.js](#start-in-nodejs) · [Cases](#choose-a-case) · [Evidence](#inspect-the-evidence) · [Depth](#formalization-depth) · [Submit a case](https://github.com/arxohq/arxo-fide-chess/issues/new) · [Source repository](https://github.com/arxohq/arxo-fide-chess)

This is an independent open-source teaching and research demonstration. For an actual chess ruling, use the authentic FIDE Laws and the competent arbiter. Source text and model scope are pinned; the package does not claim general chess-engine capability or complete formalization.

## Start in Node.js

Requirements: **Node.js 20+**. The example uses ES modules; keep the `.mjs`
extension. This recipe was checked on macOS arm64 with Node.js 20.20.2 on
14 October 2026. No global CLI, Git clone or MCP client is needed for this route.

Create a fresh directory, open a terminal there, then run:

```sh
npm init -y
npm install --ignore-scripts @arxo/canon-fide-chess@0.1.0 @arxo/law@0.4.3
```

Save this as `example.mjs`, then run `node example.mjs`:

```js
import { open } from '@arxo/law';
import { loadModel } from '@arxo/canon-fide-chess/chess';
import { game, white, getCaseInput } from '@arxo/canon-fide-chess/examples/arbiter';

const model = await loadModel();
const chess = await open(model.spec, {
  offline: true,
  local: { packages: { [model.spec]: model.package } },
});

const input = getCaseInput('SecondIllegal');
const loss = await chess.truth('game_lost_by', [game, white], input);
const draw = await chess.truth('game_drawn', [game], input);
console.log(loss.evaluationStatus, loss.truthStatus); // COMPUTED, TRUE_ONLY
console.log(draw.evaluationStatus, draw.truthStatus); // COMPUTED, NEITHER
```

The two output lines are **loss**, then **draw**:

```text
COMPUTED TRUE_ONLY
COMPUTED NEITHER
```

`COMPUTED` means the query was evaluated. `TRUE_ONLY` means it has positive
support and no negative support. `NEITHER` means neither polarity is supported;
it does not establish that the proposition is false.

Now replace only `getCaseInput('SecondIllegal')` with
`getCaseInput('SecondIllegalNoMate')` and run `node example.mjs` again:

```text
REQUIRES_JUDGMENT NEITHER
COMPUTED TRUE_ONLY
```

The second line now establishes a draw. This case supplies the fact that the
opponent cannot checkmate by any legal series. The separate loss query still
requests an arbiter's assessment because other reachable loss grounds remain
unresolved. Read both status fields; `REQUIRES_JUDGMENT` identifies an assessment
the model does not decide on its own.

To try another retained episode, choose a name from [the case table](#choose-a-case).
To propose your own episode, [open an issue](https://github.com/arxohq/arxo-fide-chess/issues/new)
with the case facts, legal date, query, package/runtime versions, output and the
FIDE clause or model rule you think should give a different answer. Use a
fictional or anonymized case.

The SDK executes the rules through `@arxo/law-engine@0.5.3`. Installation alone does not register this distribution in the SDK's automatic canon resolver: keep the explicit `local.packages` handoff above. The loader implements no chess decisions or formulas.

## Use as an MCP server

The separate native MCP wrapper runs the same pinned model over stdio:

```sh
npx -y @arxo/mcp-fide-chess@0.1.0
```

Node.js 20+, Linux x64 or macOS arm64. [Client configuration, HTTP endpoint, inputs and limitations](docs/mcp.md) · [OCI recipe](docs/mcp-release.md) · [npm recipe](docs/mcp-npm-release.md) · [Accepted delivery](docs/mcp-release.md#accepted-delivery--14-october-2026). This MCP delivery is separate from the Node.js route above.

## Choose a case

| `getCaseInput(name)` | Episode | Checked question and result |
|---|---|---|
| `TouchIntentUnknown` | A movable own piece; intentional touch not adjudicated | `must_move_first_touched_piece`: `REQUIRES_JUDGMENT / NEITHER` |
| `FirstIllegal` | One completed illegal move | Loss: `REQUIRES_JUDGMENT / NEITHER`; draw: `COMPUTED / NEITHER` |
| `SecondIllegal` | Two illegal moves under the model's specified closure | Loss: `COMPUTED / TRUE_ONLY` |
| `SecondIllegalNoMate` | Two illegal moves; inability to checkmate established | Draw: `COMPUTED / TRUE_ONLY` |
| `FlagFall` | Flag observed, time control not completed, mate possible | Loss: `COMPUTED / TRUE_ONLY` |
| `FlagFallNoMate` | The same flag; inability to checkmate established | Draw: `COMPUTED / TRUE_ONLY` |
| `RapidFirstIllegal` | Rapid 15+10; first illegal move | Opponent receives 60 seconds; 120-second query is `NEITHER` |
| `BlitzFirstIllegalCompetitive` | Blitz 3+2 under competitive rules B.2 | Opponent receives 120 seconds; 60-second query is `NEITHER` |
| `ShortOfTimeRecording` | Standard chess, no increment, 240 seconds left | `must_record_moves`: `COMPUTED / FALSE_ONLY` |
| `DeviceWarning` | Electronic device evident; arbiter gave a warning | Loss and differing-penalty queries: `COMPUTED / TRUE_ONLY` |

All 18 original case/query expectations are retained and checked. The fixture export provides `caseNames`, `game`, `white`, `black`, `king`, `CaseName` and `getCaseInput(name)`. Each call returns an independent copy; an unknown name throws `RangeError`.

## Facts and arbiter judgments

`getCaseInput` preserves the CLI's canonical assertions, constants, context and options. The loader supplies neither absent facts nor adjudications. The model's explicitly declared closures are part of its rules; they are not a general assumption that a missing fact is false.

For touch-move, use the two declared arguments — player and piece:

import { loadModel } from '@arxo/cano

readme.markdown:
# jira-easy-mcp

Another Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for Jira, without Auth token. Provides tools for complete Jira automation including issues, projects, boards, sprints, comments, worklogs, and more.

> **Tested on:** Jira Server / Data Center 7.13, 8.20, 9.12 and 10.3 (every tool, automated, see [Development & Testing](#development--testing))

---

## 🔑 Why This MCP?

**Works with Basic Authentication (username + password)** — no API tokens required!

Most Jira MCP servers require OAuth or API tokens, which many organizations restrict or don't allow. This MCP uses **HTTP Basic Authentication**, so you can connect using just your Jira username and password. Perfect for:

- 🏢 **Enterprise environments** where admins don't allow API token creation
- 🔒 **Self-hosted Jira Server** instances without OAuth configured
- ⚡ **Quick setup** without going through IT approval processes

---

## Quick Start

### VS Code (Workspace Configuration)

Create `.vscode/mcp.json` in your workspace root:

```json
{
  "servers": {
    "jira": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "jira-easy-mcp"],
      "env": {
        "JIRA_BASE_URL": "https://your-jira-instance.com",
        "JIRA_USERNAME": "your-username",
        "JIRA_PASSWORD": "your-password",
        "JIRA_PROJECTS_FILTER": "ABC,DEF,XYZ",
        "JIRA_RESPONSE_FORMAT": "JSON"
      }
    }
  }
}
```
Add to your VS Code settings for accessing in all workspaces.

> **Note:** `JIRA_PROJECTS_FILTER` and `JIRA_RESPONSE_FORMAT` are optional. Projects filter limits access to specified projects. Response format can be `JSON` (default) or `TOON` (text-oriented notation).

### Claude Code

```bash
claude mcp add jira \
  -e JIRA_BASE_URL=https://your-jira-instance.com \
  -e JIRA_USERNAME=your-username \
  -e JIRA_PASSWORD=your-password \
  -- npx -y jira-easy-mcp
```

### Codex CLI

Add to `~/.codex/config.toml`:

```toml
[mcp_servers.jira]
command = "npx"
args = ["-y", "jira-easy-mcp"]
env = { JIRA_BASE_URL = "https://your-jira-instance.com", JIRA_USERNAME = "your-username", JIRA_PASSWORD = "your-password" }
```

### Other clients

**Cursor:** `~/.cursor/mcp.json` or `.cursor/mcp.json` (use `"mcpServers": { ... }` wrapper)  
**Windsurf:** Add to your Windsurf MCP settings (use `"mcpServers": { ... }` wrapper)  
**Claude Desktop:** Edit `claude_desktop_config.json` (macOS: `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/`, Windows: `%APPDATA%\Claude\`; use `"mcpServers": { ... }` wrapper)  
**Gemini CLI:** `~/.gemini/settings.json` (use `"mcpServers": { ... }` wrapper)

All use the same `command`, `args`, and `env` configuration as VS Code above.

> **Windows:** if the client cannot start `npx`, use `"command": "cmd"` with `"args": ["/c", "npx", "-y", "jira-easy-mcp"]`.
>
> **Tool limits:** some clients (notably Cursor) cap how many tools they send to the model, historically around 40 across all servers. This server has 41; turn off the ones you don't need in the client's MCP settings.

### Credentials from the OS keychain (optional)

To keep your password out of config files, omit `JIRA_USERNAME`/`JIRA_PASSWORD` and store a credential under the service name `JiraMCP`:

- **macOS:** `security add-generic-password -s JiraMCP -a your-username -w` (prompts for the password; on first start macOS asks to allow `node` to read it)
- **Windows:** `cmdkey /generic:JiraMCP /user:your-username /pass` (use `/generic`, not `/add`)

If several accounts are stored, set `JIRA_USERNAME` to choose one. When both `JIRA_USERNAME` and `JIRA_PASSWORD` are set, they are used and the keychain is not read. Keychain support uses the optional `keytar` package; if it can't be installed on your machine, use the environment variables.

---

## Common Use Cases

| Task | Tool | Example Prompt |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Search issues** | `jira_search` | "Search for all open bugs assigned to me in project ABC" |
| **Get issue details** | `jira_get_issue` | "Show me the details of issue ABC-123" |
| **View issue images** | `jira_get_issue_images` | "Show me the screenshots attached to ABC-123" |
| **Upload attachment** | `jira_upload_attachment` | "Attach /Users/me/Desktop/error.png to ABC-123" |
| **Create issue** | `jira_create_issue` | "Create a new bug in project ABC with title 'Login button not working'" |
| **Update issue** | `jira_update_issue` | "Change the priority of ABC-123 to High and assign it to john.doe" |
| **Edit custom fields** | `jira_update_issue` + `jira_get_edit_meta` | "Set Severity on ABC-123 to Critical" (unique name or `customfield_` id) |
| **Add comment** | `jira_add_comment` | "Add a comment to ABC-123 saying 'Fix deployed to staging'" |
| **Change status** | `jira_transition_issue` | "Move ABC-123 to Done" |
| **Log time** | `jira_add_worklog` | "Log 2 hours of work on ABC-123 for yesterday" |
| **List projects** | `jira_get_projects` | "Show me all projects I have access to" |
| **View sprints** | `jira_get_sprints` | "What's in the current sprint for project ABC?" |
| **Link issues** | `jira_create_link` | "Link ABC-123 as blocking ABC-124" |
| **Generate filter URL** | `jira_generate_filter_url` | "Create a shareable link for all open bugs updated in the last 7 days" |

---

## Testing with MCP Inspector

The MCP Inspector provides a web UI to test all tools interactively:

```bash
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector npx jira-easy-mcp
```

This opens a browser at `http://localhost:6274` where you can:

- View all available tools
- Test each tool with custom parameters
- See the raw JSON responses

> **Note:** Put these values inside inspector UI before connecting: `JIRA_BASE_URL`, `JIRA_USERNAME`, `JIRA_PASSWORD`.

---

## Custom fields

Jira REST API v2 identifies custom fields by id (`customfield_10006`). Values are the raw REST payload for that field type. Display names work only when they are unique (exact, case-sensitive) on the relevant screen.

### Read (`jira_get_issue`)

Default response: system fields plus custom fi

readme.markdown:
# MCP Browser

Claude, Cursor and other MCP clients cannot open Reddit, X, LinkedIn or Facebook. Those sites block AI fetchers, so you end up reading the threads yourself and pasting them in. MCP Browser is a Mac app that lets your AI read those sites through your own Chrome login, so it sees exactly what you see and answers with links. It also reads your Search Console, Google Analytics and Microsoft Clarity data. No API keys, no OAuth setup.

Website: [webmatrices.com/mcpbrowser](https://webmatrices.com/mcpbrowser)

| Before | After |
|---|---|
| ![Claude fails to fetch a Reddit thread](docs/before.png) | ![Claude reads the same thread through MCP Browser](docs/after.png) |

## Install

Mac with Apple Silicon. Download, open, sign in, press Connect.

1. Download the app from the [latest release](https://github.com/Bishwas-py/mcpbrowser/releases/latest) or from [webmatrices.com/mcpbrowser](https://webmatrices.com/mcpbrowser). Drag it into Applications and open it. The app is signed and notarized.
2. Sign in with a free Webmatrices account.
3. Press **Connect** next to your AI client. The app detects what you have installed and writes the MCP config for it. No JSON to edit.

Supported clients: Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, Zed, VS Code.

Other ways in:

```bash
brew install --cask bishwas-py/tap/mcpbrowser
```

Claude Desktop only: download the `.mcpb` file from the [latest release](https://github.com/Bishwas-py/mcpbrowser/releases/latest) and double-click it. No app needed.

## What it reads

| Source | What you can ask for | Runs through |
|---|---|---|
| [Reddit](https://webmatrices.com/mcpbrowser/reddit-mcp) | Search, subreddit feeds, a post with its comment tree, a user's history | Direct |
| [X / Twitter](https://webmatrices.com/mcpbrowser/twitter-mcp) | Search tweets, a tweet with replies, a user's timeline | Your Chrome login |
| [LinkedIn](https://webmatrices.com/mcpbrowser/linkedin-mcp) | Search posts, your home feed, comments on a post, your creator analytics | Your Chrome login |
| [Facebook](https://webmatrices.com/mcpbrowser/facebook-mcp) | Search public posts, a page's recent posts, your page insights | Your Chrome login |
| [Pinterest](https://webmatrices.com/mcpbrowser/pinterest-mcp) | Search pins, boards, a user's pins, trends with demographics, pin images for vision | Your Chrome login |
| [Medium](https://webmatrices.com/mcpbrowser/medium-mcp) | Search articles, tag feeds, a writer's latest | Login for search, feeds are direct |
| [Dev.to](https://webmatrices.com/mcpbrowser/dev-to-mcp) | Search, trending, an article with comments, a user's articles | Direct |
| [BlackHatWorld](https://webmatrices.com/mcpbrowser/blackhatworld-mcp) | Search, a thread with replies, latest posts | Your Chrome login |
| Google News and Trends | Trending terms by region, news search, top stories, by topic | Direct |
| [Google Search Console](https://webmatrices.com/mcpbrowser/google-search-console-mcp) | Clicks, impressions, CTR and position by query, page, country, device or date | Your Google login |
| [Google Analytics and Clarity](https://webmatrices.com/mcpbrowser/google-analytics-mcp) | GA4 pages, traffic, users, events. Clarity sessions, dead clicks, scroll depth | Your Google and Microsoft logins |

# KEPTA — the memory for AI systems

## Your AI forgets everything. Every chat starts from zero.

**KEPTA is the fix: one local, encrypted memory that every AI reads and writes — Claude, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Cline, any MCP client, and scripts over HTTP. No cloud. No account. One file you own.**

Everything an AI system learns goes into an encrypted knowledge base on your own computer — and every AI recalls it in milliseconds, however long the context grows. Documents, decisions, client knowledge, whole chat histories: remembered, linked, contradicted, superseded — never lost.

This repository is the **source-available core** (BUSL-1.1 — every line public, converts to AGPL-3.0-or-later four years after each release): the memory engine, the MCP server, the HTTP API — and the Python client, which is MIT so any Python project can embed it. **Everything that makes the memory smart lives in this free engine. There are no tiers inside the memory — nothing is held back to sell anything.**

Questions, security feedback or benchmark critique? → **[Discussions](https://github.com/DamianTodorovic/kepta/discussions)**

```mermaid

    direction TB
    A["Claude Desktop · Claude Code"]
    B["Cursor · Gemini CLICline · Codex · Zed"]
    C["Your scripts"]
  end
  subgraph KEPTA["KEPTA — this repository"]
    direction TB
    M["MCP server8 tools · stdio + Streamable HTTP"]
    G["HTTP API · 32 routesPython client · CLI"]
    E["Memory enginehybrid retrieval: FTS5 + vectors + graphRRF fusion → local rerank"]
  end
  D[("One encrypted fileSQLCipher 4 · AES-256~/.kepta/kepta.db")]
  K["OS keychainthe key never leaves"]
  A --> M
  B --> M
  C --> G
  G --> E
  M --> E
  E --> D
  D -.-> K
```

---

## ⚡ One command, every AI client

Needs **Node 22.13 or newer** (`package.json` → `engines`) on the machine you install on; npm has prebuilt SQLite binaries for Node 22, 24 and 26.

```bash
npx -y kepta-mcp demo          # six scenes in a throwaway database — nothing of yours is touched
npx -y kepta-mcp setup         # connects Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, VS Code, Gemini CLI, Cline and Roo Code
npx -y kepta-mcp remember "Client Miller signs renewals in December."   # write a note from the terminal, no AI client needed
npx -y kepta-mcp recall "who signs renewals"                            # read it back: 1 match — ranked by relevance
npx -y kepta-mcp stats         # size, encryption state, top tags
npx -y kepta-mcp timeline "miller"                                     # what was true, and when
npx -y kepta-mcp import chatgpt <export-folder>   # bring your ChatGPT history with you (export → extract → import)
```

What those two lines answer, verbatim — `kepta-mcp` 3.2.0 from the registry on 10.10.2026, a
throwaway `HOME`, an empty memory:

```text
$ npx -y kepta-mcp remember "Client Miller signs renewals in December."
✓ remembered — Client Miller signs renewals in December.
  type: semantic · id: k-mv2mghs9-fdf75c17

$ npx -y kepta-mcp recall "who signs renewals"
1 match — ranked by relevance

1. Client Miller signs renewals in December. · semantic · today
  Client Miller signs renewals in December.
  #remember
```

A **note** is one thing your memory holds — `remember` writes one by hand, your AI client writes the same kind through the `memory_save` tool. Then tell your AI something worth keeping — and watch it arrive. Details in the [Quick start](#-quick-start).

---

---

## 🖥️ Or download the desktop app

**The core has no window of its own: its interface is your AI client.** If you want a window, that is the free desktop app — same engine, same encrypted file, same key — and it is downloadable from the releases of this repository. For teams and organizations there is KEPTA Enterprise by agreement. These three sentences are the whole answer; every document here says the same.

The app brings the memory browser, hybrid search with retrieval provenance, the knowledge graph, time travel, dossiers and a chat that reads the memory. Download the DMG for your Mac from the [latest release](https://github.com/DamianTodorovic/kepta/releases/latest) (Apple Silicon or Intel) and drag it into Applications. The build is ad-hoc signed and not notarised, so macOS asks a single time. Two ways through, and both work on every macOS version: `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/KEPTA.app`, or **System Settings → Privacy & Security** → the KEPTA message → **Open Anyway**. Once, then never again. Older guides say right-click → *Open*; Apple removed that route in macOS 15 and it does nothing on current systems. (What runs from this repository has no window: `npm run dev` starts the HTTP API and its `POST /mcp` — a service on your machine, not an interface.)

The app is free, like everything in this repository. KEPTA Enterprise (team and tenant memory, audit chain, human review, point-in-time recovery) is licensed by agreement — [write to me on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/damian-todorovic-244235434).

KEPTA is not a feature inside one app — it is a memory layer that outlives every model, every app and every context window. Three doors lead into the same encrypted file:

| Door | What uses it |
|---|---|
| **MCP** — 8 tools, stdio (npm binary and container) + Streamable HTTP (this repository, run from source) | Every MCP client: Claude, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Cline, Codex, Zed, your own agents |

**Free means free:** €0, forever — no account, no licence key, no daily limit, no tier inside the memory, nothing locked to sell you later. readme.markdown:
Brain Memory

  
  
  

A hierarchical, file-system-based memory plugin for AI coding agents. Inspired by human neuroscience — memories are organized into deep nested life-domain categories, connected via associative networks, strengthened through spaced recall, and naturally decay over time.

One hosted **MCP connector** reaches every major agent and chat app — **Claude Code**, **OpenAI Codex CLI**, **OpenCode**, **GitHub Copilot CLI**, **Kilo**, the **Claude.ai** apps, **ChatGPT**, **Google Antigravity** (Gemini CLI's successor), **OpenClaw** / **NVIDIA NemoClaw**, **Hermes Agent**, and **Goose**. Prefer a free, local-first install? The native plugin runs entirely from `~/.brain/` on Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Copilot CLI, Kilo, and Antigravity — and dedicated [native integrations](integrations/) plug the same brain into OpenClaw and Hermes as their memory engine.

```
~/.brain/
├── professional/
│   └── companies/
│       └── acme-corp/
│           └── projects/
│               └── alpha-launch.md        ⚡ 0.88
├── personal/
│   └── education/
│       └── typescript-generics.md         ⚡ 0.72
├── social/
│   └── communities/
│       └── open-source-contrib.md         ⚡ 0.65
└── family/
    └── events/
        └── annual-reunion-planning.md     ⚡ 0.55
```

## Why Brain Memory?

Existing AI memory solutions use flat databases with tag-based retrieval. Brain Memory is different:

- **The directory tree IS the semantic structure** — `professional/companies/acme/projects/` tells the agent everything about context without vector search
- **Human-inspectable** — Browse your "brain" in any file explorer
- **Git-friendly** — Full version history of how memories evolve
- **Strength + decay** — Recalled memories get stronger, forgotten ones fade. Just like your brain
- **Recall receipts** — Memory that visibly fires: every answer shaped by a memory ends with a one-line attributable receipt (`◉ memory: "<title>" (<type>, <age>)`), minted by the engine so it can't be hallucinated
- **Provenance-bounded trust** — Every memory records where it came from (`user`, `agent-inferred`, `tool-output`, `external`), and recall weighs it: a fact planted by a web page or tool output is down-ranked, flagged `low_trust`, marked `⚠` on its receipt, and can never outrank what you said directly — no matter how many copies of it get written. And because memories are plain files, Brain records a **SHA-256 baseline** of each one at write time — so `brain audit` also catches a memory edited *outside* any write path, the one poisoning route every write-path defense is blind to
- **Bitemporal — it knows *when* a fact was true** — Every memory separates record time (when the brain learned it) from valid time (`valid_from` / `valid_until`, when it was actually true). So "we deploy to Fly.io" and "we deploy to Render" aren't a contradiction to guess between — they're one fact with a boundary. `brain recall "deploy target" --as-of 2026-03-01` answers what was true in March; `--as-known-of` answers what the brain knew then. Facts that stopped being true are demoted and marked `⌛ expired`, never silently served as current
- **Deterministic recall — every agent ranks identically** — Scoring is arithmetic over files, not a model call: TF-IDF/BM25 relevance, decayed strength, spreading activation, context match, salience. Claude, Codex, and Gemini asking the same question of the same brain get the *same* ranking, in the same order, offline. No embedding-model version can silently reshuffle what your agent remembers
- **Associative network** — Memories link to each other with weighted connections. Recalling one activates related ones automatically
- **Context-dependent recall** — Memories encoded in a similar context to the current session are scored higher
- **Spaced reinforcement** — Memories recalled after longer intervals get bigger boosts, cramming produces diminishing returns
- **Cognitive types** — Episodic, semantic, and procedural memories each decay differently, just like in the brain
- **Always-present knowledge** — Pin critical conventions and preferences so they load every session, bypassing recall and never decaying — the facts your agent must never miss
- **Procedural skills** — Reusable how-to workflows with progressive disclosure, learned automatically from repeated experience and exportable to your agent's native skills
- **On-demand depth** — Subcategories are created as needed, not pre-defined
- **Consolidation** — Weak related memories merge into stronger combined knowledge
- **Zero dependencies — and measured, not assumed** — Pure file I/O: no database, no server, no embedding model. That is a deliberate result, not a shortcut. On our hardest retrieval scenario (1,021 memories, 1,000 plausible distractors) a real embedding model ranked the target memories *worse* than BM25 — see the [retrieval-only pilot](benchmark/README.md#retrieval-only-pilot-no-agent-no-llm-spend)

## Install

There are two ways to give an agent its brain. They are complementary — most people end up with both:

| Path | Reaches | Storage | Cost | Best for |
|------|---------|---------|------|----------|
| **Hosted MCP connector** | Every MCP-capable host (Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenCode, Copilot CLI, Kilo, Claude.ai apps, ChatGPT, Antigravity, OpenClaw, Hermes, Goose) | Brain Cloud (hosted) | account | One connector, everywhere — including web & mobile chat |
| **Local-first native plugin** | The current CLIs (Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenCode, Copilot CLI, Kilo, Antigravity) | `~/.brain/` on your machine | free | Zero-config ambient memory, no account, files you own |
| **[Assistant integrations](integrations/)** | OpenClaw / NVIDIA NemoClaw (memory-slot plugin), Hermes Agent (memory provider) | `~/.brain/` on your machine | free | Your always-on personal assistant sharing one brain with your coding agents |

### 1. Universal path — the hosted MCP connector

Brain Cloud exposes a single remote MCP server (streamable-HTTP + OAuth) at *

description: Read, write and scan process memory, Cheat Engine style, on Windows, Linux and macOS.

readme.markdown: # PyMemoryEditor A pure-Python library (built on [ctypes](https://docs.python.org/3/library/ctypes.html)) that lets you **inspect, modify and search the memory of any running process in a few lines of Python** — Cheat Engine workflows on Windows, Linux and macOS! --- Read, write and scan the memory of any process — straight from Python. One unified API. Three operating systems. No C compiler. No native build step. Runs on Windows · Linux · macOS — 32-bit and 64-bit. Tweak a value in a running game · inspect a live program's state · harvest data straight from RAM. --- ## Install ```bash pip install PyMemoryEditor ``` To also install the bundled GUI app (a Cheat Engine-style scanner), use the `app` extra: ```bash pip install "PyMemoryEditor[app]" pymemoryeditor ``` For faster scans on large processes, add the `speed` extra. It pulls in NumPy and automatically vectorizes the numeric scan comparison loop — ~10–30× faster on selective scans: ```bash pip install "PyMemoryEditor[speed]" ``` To let an AI assistant drive the library over the Model Context Protocol, use the `mcp` extra (see [below](#let-an-ai-assistant-do-it-mcp)): ```bash pip install "PyMemoryEditor[mcp]" ``` 📖 Full guide at **[Read the Docs](https://pymemoryeditor.readthedocs.io)**. --- ## See it in action ```python from PyMemoryEditor import OpenProcess with OpenProcess(name="game.exe") as process: # Scan the whole process for every address holding the value 100. for address in process.search_by_value(int, value=100): print(f"Found at 0x{address:X}") # Read the current value, then write a new one back. current = process.read_int(address) process.write_int(address, current + 500) ``` That's it — read, write or scan another process in three lines, the same way on every platform. --- ## Let an AI assistant do it (MCP) PyMemoryEditor ships a **Model Context Protocol server**, so an AI assistant can run the whole loop itself: > *"Find the health value in my game. It's 100 right now."* > > It scans, asks you to take damage, refines the matches, and hands you the address. ```bash pip install "PyMemoryEditor[mcp]" claude mcp add pymemoryeditor -- pymemoryeditor-mcp ``` Or in any client that reads `mcpServers` JSON (Claude Desktop, editors, …): ```json { "mcpServers": { "pymemoryeditor": { "command": "pymemoryeditor-mcp", "args": [] } } } ``` Fourteen tools cover the full workflow, with scan results kept server-side behind a handle, so a 40 000-hit first scan costs a few tokens instead of your whole context. Read the [MCP guide](https://pymemoryeditor.readthedocs.io/en/latest/mcp.html) to learn more. --- ## 📖 Documentation Full documentation lives at **[pymemoryeditor.readthedocs.io](https://pymemoryeditor.readthedocs.io)** — installation, the Cheat Engine workflow, every method and parameter, the GUI app guide, platform notes and troubleshooting. A quick map of where to go: Quick StartOpen a process, read, write and run your first scan. Searching memoryValue scans, ranges, refining results, the Cheat Engine loop. Pattern scanFind code/data with byte signatures (AOB) and regex. PointersMulti-level pointer chains and the live RemotePointer. Pointer scanFind static pointers that survive ASLR. The GUI appThe bundled Cheat Engine-style scanner. The MCP serverLet an AI assistant drive the scan/refine loop. API referenceEvery public class, method and parameter. Platform notesPermissions and quirks on Windows, Linux and macOS. TroubleshootingCommon errors and how to fix them. --- ## What can I build with this? - 🎮 **Game modding & speedrunning tools** — the classic Cheat Engine use case. - 🔬 **Debugging & introspection** — inspect live state without attaching a debugger. - 📊 **Observability tooling** — sample variables in a running process for telemetry. - 🔐 **Security & reverse-engineering research** — on systems you own or are authorized to test. - 🎓 **Learning** — the bundled app is a great teaching tool for how memory scanning works. > [!NOTE] > **Responsible use.** PyMemoryEditor talks to other processes through OS-level APIs. > Only point it at processes you own or have explicit permission to inspect. --- ## 🤝 Contributing Pull requests, bug reports and feature ideas are very welcome. Read [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](https://github.com/JeanExtreme002/PyMemoryEditor/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) for the development setup, test layout and the small set of platform-specific quirks to be aware of. If PyMemoryEditor helped your project, please ⭐ the repo — it's the easiest way to support the work and to help others discover the library. --- ## License Released under the [MIT License](https://github.com/JeanExtreme002/PyMemoryEditor/blob/main/LICENSE) — free for personal and commercial use.

readme.markdown:
# yab-mcp

The MCP server of Yab, Yet Another Browser, for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and any MCP client.

Yab, Yet Another Browser, is a free WebKit browser for the Mac. With this server, any agent gets one real browser on your Mac: the one you're signed in to. Your agent opens tabs of its own beside yours, reads pages as text, clicks, types and fills forms with your sign-ins, your cookies and your IP. There is no cloud browser, no debug port and no Chrome to set up, and it's free. A press on Send, Pay, Delete and the like waits for your yes on a card in Yab, unless you chose Bypass in Yab's settings: the browser holds that yes, not the model. Saved passwords are filled by Yab and never shown to the agent. Agent tabs live in a window off screen and come in front of you only when you ask. With Yab closed, the first call opens it hidden, with no window and no Dock tile, and it quits after half an hour with nothing to do. `yab serve` keeps it running that way.

[Download Yab](https://yetanotherbrowser.com/dl?ref=github) · [For developers](https://yetanotherbrowser.com/developers) · [Manual](https://yetanotherbrowser.com/manual)

## Remote assistants (0.2.0 preview)

On the assistant's own computer, run `npx yab-mcp login --client dots`.
When Yab's Connect flow supplies a nonce, add `--nonce` with that value.
It prints the code and returns immediately; a background process saves the
connection after the person allows it in Yab.
Yab on the Mac shows the eight-character code under Settings > AI > Assistants.
After the person allows it there, choose who does the work:

- **Direct browser control:** configure your assistant's MCP server with command
  `npx` and args `["-y", "yab-mcp", "--remote"]`. The assistant calls `open`,
  `snapshot`, `click`, `type`, etc. itself, using its own model/account.
  `--remote` bridges JSON-RPC over stdio; it does not accept a natural-language
  prompt or start a Yab model run. Calling the `task` MCP tool still delegates.
- **Delegation:** `npx yab-mcp task "Find a table for Friday"` starts a separate
  agent using the model selected for Tasks in Yab on the Mac. ChatGPT (via Codex)
  consumes the user's ChatGPT limits; Claude uses their Claude plan instead.
  Choose this when you intend to use that plan, including from a shell-only bot.
  It prints its session ID and returns; run `npx yab-mcp status SESSION` for the
  next update, or `npx yab-mcp status` for the newest task after a Mac reconnects.
  Repeat until it says done.

Both modes keep the assistant's existing account access and approval settings.
The connection token stays in `~/.config/yab-mcp/auth.json` (mode 0600), or the
path in `YAB_MCP_AUTH_FILE`. When the home folder is read-only, as on some bots'
computers, it goes to the first writable of `/workspace/shared/.yab-mcp/`,
`/workspace/.yab-mcp/` and `.yab-mcp/` in the current folder. If the computer
ends the background process that waits for the person's Allow, the next
`task`, `status` or `--remote` finishes connecting.
`YAB_MCP_URL` selects a test server; production uses `https://yab-sync.21st.workers.dev`.
Plain `npx yab-mcp` starts the local app's MCP server.

## Requirements

- A Mac with macOS 15.4 or later.
- Yab, free: [download](https://yetanotherbrowser.com/dl?ref=github). It updates itself.
- Agents allowed in Yab: Settings › AI › Agents › Let agents use Yab. Until then, every call says so.
- Node.js 18 or later, for `npx`. A client can also run Yab directly, without Node: see [Without Node](#without-node).

Chrome is your main browser? Yab can still be the one your agents use, usually closed. `yab import chrome` brings Chrome's sign-ins into Yab after you say yes in Yab, so your agent hits fewer sign-in pages.

Already use Yab? Settings › Developers adds it to Claude Code and Codex with one click, and Copy Config gives the JSON for any other client. You don't need this package for that.

## Install

### Claude Code

The plugin brings the tools and Yab's skill:

```
/plugin marketplace add yetanotherbrowser/yab-mcp
/plugin install yab@yab-mcp
```

From a shell: `claude plugin marketplace add yetanotherbrowser/yab-mcp`, then `claude plugin install yab@yab-mcp`.

Only the tools:

```sh
claude mcp add --scope user yab-browser -- npx -y yab-mcp
```

If Yab's Settings › Developers already added Yab to Claude Code, skip this: you'd have the same tools twice.

### Codex

The plugin, tools and skill:

```sh
codex plugin marketplace add yetanotherbrowser/yab-mcp
codex plugin add yab@yab-mcp
```

Or only the tools, in `~/.codex/config.toml`:

```toml
[mcp_servers.yab-browser]
command = "npx"
args = ["-y", "yab-mcp"]
tool_timeout_sec = 900
default_tools_approval_mode = "approve"
```

`tool_timeout_sec` lets a call wait up to 15 minutes while Yab asks you something; the plugin keeps Codex's default of 5. `default_tools_approval_mode` stops Codex asking before every Yab tool; Yab still asks you before Send, Pay and Delete. Leave it out if you want Codex to ask too.

### Cursor

Or add it to `~/.cursor/mcp.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "yab-browser": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "yab-mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

### VS Code

```sh
code --add-mcp '{"name":"yab-browser","command":"npx","args":["-y","yab-mcp"]}'
```

Or in `.vscode/mcp.json`:

```json
{
  "servers": {
    "yab-browser": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "yab-mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

### Windsurf (Devin Desktop)

In `~/.config/devin/mcp_config.json` (older Windsurf builds: `~/.codeium/windsurf/mcp_config.json`):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "yab-browser": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "yab-mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

Download `yab-mcp-<version>.mcpb` from [Releases](https://github.com/yetanotherbrowser/yab-mcp/releases) and open it: Claude Desktop installs it as an extension. Or add this to `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json`:

tools.name: list_federal_holidays
tools.description: List the eleven U.S. federal holidays for one calendar year (2021 through 2100): each holiday's name, its actual date and weekday, the date it is observed when it falls on a weekend (Saturday moves to the Friday before, Sunday to the Monday after), and the rule that sets it, from 5 U.S.C. 6103. Use it to answer which days federal offices close in a year.

inputs.name: year
inputs.description: Calendar year, 2021 through 2100.

tools.name: next_federal_holidays
tools.description: Find the next one to eleven U.S. federal holidays observed on or after a date, with each one's observed date and how many calendar days away it is. Without from_date it starts from today's date in America/New_York and says which date it used.

inputs.name: from_date
inputs.description: Start looking on this date, inclusive, written YYYY-MM-DD (for example 2026-11-26). Covers 2021 through 2100.

inputs.name: count
inputs.description: How many upcoming holidays to return, 1 to 11. Defaults to 1.

tools.name: check_business_day
tools.description: Check whether a date is a U.S. business day (a weekday that is not an observed federal holiday). Returns the weekday, the holiday observed that day if any, and the business days just before and just after it.

inputs.name: date
inputs.description: The date to check, written YYYY-MM-DD (for example 2026-11-26). Covers 2021 through 2100.

tools.name: add_business_days
tools.description: Move a number of U.S. business days forward or backward from a date, skipping weekends and observed federal holidays, for due dates, delivery windows and notice periods. The start date is not counted: 1 business day after a Friday is the next Monday, or Tuesday when that Monday is a holiday. Returns the resulting date and every holiday it skipped. Up to 1,000 business days either way.

inputs.name: start_date
inputs.description: The date to count from. It is not counted itself, written YYYY-MM-DD (for example 2026-11-26). Covers 2021 through 2100.

inputs.name: business_days
inputs.description: Business days to move, -1000 to 1000. Negative counts backward. 0 returns the start date if it is a business day, otherwise the next one.

tools.name: count_business_days
tools.description: Count the U.S. business days between two dates, both dates included, leaving out weekends and observed federal holidays. Returns the business day count, the weekend days, and each holiday that fell in the span. Spans up to 3,660 calendar days.

inputs.name: start_date
inputs.description: First date of the span, counted if it is a business day, written YYYY-MM-DD (for example 2026-11-26). Covers 2021 through 2100.

inputs.name: end_date
inputs.description: Last date of the span, counted if it is a business day, written YYYY-MM-DD (for example 2026-11-26). Covers 2021 through 2100.

# Small Business MCP Starter Kit by Modern Mustard Seed

Ship a remote MCP connector for Claude that is built to pass Anthropic's directory review on the first try.

This kit is the set of patterns Modern Mustard Seed uses for the connectors it runs in production, pulled out into a clean Next.js project you can fork:

- **A route template** on Next.js App Router and [`mcp-handler`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/mcp-handler), serving Streamable HTTP at one URL per connector, with no redirect.
- **Tool conventions enforced at load time**: a title, `readOnlyHint` or `destructiveHint` on every tool, snake_case names of 64 characters or fewer, and descriptions that describe instead of steer. Break a rule and `pnpm test` fails, long before a reviewer sees it.
- **Specific error messages** instead of "Bad Request", and **output size caps** under Claude's limits.
- **Rate limiting built for Claude's shared egress range.** Every claude.ai user arrives from `160.79.104.0/21`, so nothing is keyed by IP and nothing returns HTTP 429.
- **An SSRF-safe fetch** for any tool that reads a URL a user supplied, with tests that prove a listening loopback server receives zero requests.
- **An eval harness** that runs real prompts against your live URL, with no model and no API key.
- **Docs, privacy, terms and support page templates** plus `/.well-known/security.txt`, all driven by one config file.
- **A submission checklist** mapped to the directory form's 10 steps and its seven policy acknowledgments, with every rule linked to Anthropic's documentation.
- **A worked example**: a U.S. federal holiday and business-day calendar with five read-only tools that passes all 35 of its own evals.

MIT licensed. Built by [Modern Mustard Seed](https://modernmustardseed.com).

## Working demo

The example connector runs live, deployed from this repository with no changes:

- Connector URL: `https://starter.modernmustardseed.com/holidays` (add it in Claude under **Customize > Connectors > Add custom connector**)
- Docs page reviewers read: https://starter.modernmustardseed.com/docs/holidays
- Privacy, terms and support: https://starter.modernmustardseed.com/privacy, [/terms](https://starter.modernmustardseed.com/terms), [/support](https://starter.modernmustardseed.com/support)
- Official MCP Registry entry: `com.modernmustardseed/holiday-calendar`

Run the evals against it yourself: `node eval/holidays.eval.mjs https://starter.modernmustardseed.com`

## Quickstart: 10 minutes

You need Node 22.6 or later, pnpm, and a Vercel account (any host that runs Next.js works).

**1. Make your copy.** (1 minute)

```sh
gh repo create my-connector --template ModernMustardSeed/small-business-mcp-starter --public --clone
cd my-connector
pnpm install
```

Or select **Use this template** on GitHub.

**2. Run it and prove it works.** (2 minutes)

```sh
pnpm dev
```

In a second terminal:

```sh
pnpm test
pnpm evals http://localhost:3000
```

You should see `32 pass` from the unit tests and `35 of 35 passed` from the evals. Open http://localhost:3000/docs/holidays to see the docs page reviewers read.

**3. Make it yours.** (2 minutes)

Edit `lib/site.ts`: company name, location, website, support inbox, security inbox, and the policy date. Every public page and `security.txt` read from it. Replace `app/icon.svg` and `app/apple-icon.png` with your own mark; the directory listing asks for an icon.

**4. Deploy.** (3 minutes)

Import the repository at [vercel.com/new](https://vercel.com/new), or from the terminal:

```sh
vercel deploy --prod
```

Vercel sets `VERCEL_PROJECT_PRODUCTION_URL`, which the pages use for their links. Leave Attack Challenge Mode and any bot-protection rule off for your MCP paths: they answer Claude with a challenge page.

**5. Check the deployment.** (1 minute)

```sh
pnpm preflight https://your-project.vercel.app
pnpm evals https://your-project.vercel.app
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli https://your-project.vercel.app/holidays --transport http --method tools/list
```

Preflight checks HTTPS, no redirect, no 403 or 429, every public page returning 200, the MCP handshake and the annotation rules.

**6. Try it in Claude.** (1 minute)

In Claude, open **Customize > Connectors > Add custom connector** and paste `https://your-project.vercel.app/holidays`. Ask: "An invoice dated 2026-11-20 is due in 10 business days. What date is that?" In Claude Code:

```sh
claude mcp add --transport http holidays https://your-project.vercel.app/holidays
```

## Build your own connector

1. Copy `lib/holidays/tools.ts` to `lib/<yours>/tools.ts`. Declare each tool as a `ToolSpec`: name, title, description, zod input schema, annotations, a per-minute limit, optional global limits, the fields that are safe to log, and a `run` function that returns `ok(data)` or `fail(code, sentence)`.
2. Copy `app/holidays/route.ts` to `app/<yours>/route.ts` and point it at your tools.
3. Copy `app/docs/holidays/page.tsx` to `app/docs/<yours>/page.tsx`. Keep the "For reviewers" section: you paste it into the form.
4. Rewrite `app/privacy/page.tsx` so every sentence is true of your tools: what they receive, what they read, what you keep and for how long, who else touches it.
5. Copy `eval/holidays.eval.mjs`. Write 20 to 50 cases from prompts real users type, with expected values from an authority outside your code. Include the error cases.
6. If a tool fetches a URL a user gave you, use `safeFetch` from `lib/mcp/safe-fetch.ts`. Never `fetch` a user-supplied URL directly.
7. Deploy, run `pnpm preflight` and `pnpm evals` against production, test every tool in Claude, then work through [docs/SUBMISSION-CHECKLIST.md](docs/SUBMISSION-CHECKLIST.md).

Why each pattern exists, with the rule it answers: [docs/PATTERNS.md](docs/PATTERNS.md).

## What is in the box

| Path | What it does |
|---|---|
| `app/holidays/route.ts` | The connector endpoint. One file per connector. |
| `lib/mcp/tool.ts` | `ToolSpec`, `registerTools`, `runTool`: conventions, limits, e

# iCloud Calendar MCP Server

A [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/) server that gives MCP clients access to iCloud Calendar
over CalDAV: list calendars, read, create, update, move and delete events. It works on Linux, macOS and Windows,
since it talks to iCloud directly instead of going through the macOS Calendar app.

This is a maintained fork of [zwrong/iCalendar](https://github.com/zwrong/iCalendar), itself derived from the macOS
`mcp-ical` server. See [Changes in this fork](#changes-in-this-fork).

## Tools

| Tool | Description |
|---|---|
| `list_calendars` | Names of the available calendars |
| `list_events` | Events in a date range, optionally for one calendar, sorted by start time |
| `create_event` | New event: title, times, all-day, location, notes, URL, alarms, recurrence |
| `update_event` | Change any of those fields, or move the event to another calendar |
| `delete_event` | Delete an event by identifier |
| `debug_calendar_connection` | Connection check: calendars and event counts over the last 7 days |

The `calendars://list` resource also lists the calendars. With `MCP_ICAL_READ_ONLY=true`, the three write tools are
not registered at all.

## Requirements

- Python 3.12 or later and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/)
- An Apple ID with iCloud Calendar enabled
- An **app-specific password** for that Apple ID

### App-specific password

1. Sign in to [appleid.apple.com](https://appleid.apple.com/), open **Sign-In and Security**, then
   **App-Specific Passwords**.
2. Generate a password, for example named `mcp-icloud-caldav`.

The username is your Apple ID address, which is not necessarily an `@icloud.com` address.
An app-specific password gives access to iCloud CalDAV, CardDAV and IMAP: keep it out of version control and revoke
it if it leaks.

## Installation

The package is published on PyPI as `mcp-icloud-caldav`. With [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), MCP clients can
start it directly, without a separate install step:

```bash
uvx mcp-icloud-caldav
```

`uvx` downloads the package into a cached, isolated environment on first use. To install it permanently instead:
`uv tool install mcp-icloud-caldav` (or `pipx install mcp-icloud-caldav`).

From source:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Glob0x17/mcp-icloud-caldav.git mcp-icloud-caldav
cd mcp-icloud-caldav
uv sync --no-dev
uv run mcp-icloud-caldav
```

## Configuration

Credentials are read in this order:

1. **Environment variables** (recommended)

   | Variable | Required | Default |
   |---|---|---|
   | `ICLOUD_USERNAME` | yes | |
   | `ICLOUD_PASSWORD` | yes | |
   | `CALDAV_SERVER_URL` | no | `https://caldav.icloud.com/` |

2. **`MCP_ICAL_CONFIG`**: path to a JSON file shaped like [`config.json.example`](config.json.example)
3. **`config_private.json`**, then **`config.json`**, at the repository root (kept for compatibility)

Other settings:

| Variable | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `MCP_ICAL_READ_ONLY` | `false` | `true` leaves out `create_event`, `update_event` and `delete_event` |
| `MCP_ICAL_LOG_LEVEL` | `INFO` | `TRACE`, `DEBUG`, `INFO`, `WARNING` or `ERROR`. Logs go to stderr |

The server speaks MCP over stdio and is started by the client. To check it by hand:

```bash
ICLOUD_USERNAME=you@example.com ICLOUD_PASSWORD=xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx uvx mcp-icloud-caldav
```

It waits on stdin and prints nothing on stdout.

## Client setup

Use the absolute path of `uvx` (`which uvx`) if the client cannot find it: clients often start servers without your
shell `PATH`, which shows up as `spawn uvx ENOENT`. Usual locations:

| Installed with | Path |
|---|---|
| The uv installer (Linux, macOS) | `~/.local/bin/uvx` |
| Homebrew on Apple silicon | `/opt/homebrew/bin/uvx` |
| Homebrew on Intel Macs | `/usr/local/bin/uvx` |

The command and its argument are separate fields: the command is `uvx` (or its path) and `mcp-icloud-caldav` is an
argument. A config where the command is the single string `"uvx mcp-icloud-caldav"` fails with `ENOENT`, because
the client looks for a program with that exact name, space included.

### Keeping the password out of the client config

Most clients store `env` values in clear text in their config file. A small wrapper that reads an env file avoids
that:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/.config/mcp-icloud-caldav && chmod 700 ~/.config/mcp-icloud-caldav
cat > ~/.config/mcp-icloud-caldav/env <<'EOF'
ICLOUD_USERNAME=you@example.com
ICLOUD_PASSWORD=xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx
MCP_ICAL_READ_ONLY=true
EOF
chmod 600 ~/.config/mcp-icloud-caldav/env

cat > ~/.local/bin/mcp-icloud-caldav-run <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
set -a; source "$HOME/.config/mcp-icloud-caldav/env"; set +a
exec /absolute/path/to/uvx mcp-icloud-caldav
EOF
chmod +x ~/.local/bin/mcp-icloud-caldav-run
```

Then point the client at `~/.local/bin/mcp-icloud-caldav-run`. Starting read-only and switching to `false` once reading works
is a sensible first step.

### Claude Desktop

In `claude_desktop_config.json` (Settings, Developer, Edit Config). On macOS it is
`~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "icloud-calendar": {
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["mcp-icloud-caldav"],
      "env": {
        "ICLOUD_USERNAME": "you@example.com",
        "ICLOUD_PASSWORD": "xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

or, with the wrapper, `"command": "/home/you/.local/bin/mcp-icloud-caldav-run"` and no `env`. Quit Claude Desktop
completely and start it again after editing. On macOS, server logs are in
`~/Library/Logs/Claude/mcp-server-icloud-calendar.log`.

### Claude Code

```bash
claude mcp add --scope user icloud-calendar \
  -e ICLOUD_USERNAME=you@example.com -e ICLOUD_PASSWORD=xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx \
  -- uvx mcp-icloud-caldav
```

or, with the wrapper, `claude mcp add --scope user icloud-calendar -- ~/.local/bin/mcp-icloud-caldav-run`.

Do not quote what follows `--`: `-- uvx mcp-icloud-caldav` registers `uvx` as the command and `mcp-icloud-caldav` as
it

readme.markdown:
# adrkit

**Decision memory for human- and agent-authored plans** — architecture decision
records that are machine-readable, enforceable in CI, and legible to agents,
without leaving git.

Most ADR tooling is a markdown template and a static site generator. That
*records* a decision; it doesn't make the decision *do* anything. adrkit treats a
record as **typed data with a markdown body** and adds one field — `affects` —
so a tool can answer *"which decisions govern this pull request?"* and put the
answer where the next decision is being made.

An 80-second tour, from the terminal to the pull request to the GitHub Copilot
app:

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/2ab466f9-53f0-4274-a87c-98d8d5e5ecdf

<sub>A still of the final screen. Select it to watch the 15-second recording.</sub>

On a pull request, the [governing-decisions Action](https://adrkit.dev/ci/)
posts that answer as a comment, and GitHub Copilot code review can cite a record
because it lives in the repository:

  
  

[`mbeacom/adrkit-demo`](https://github.com/mbeacom/adrkit-demo) is a small
payments-ledger repository with these pull requests open, a managed ARB queue
issue, and recordings of every command.

## Decision governance, not generated documentation

Generated knowledge systems answer *"how does the system work now?"* adrkit
answers *"what did people decide, what alternatives were rejected, and which
decisions govern this change?"*
[ADR-0037](docs/adr/0037-treat-generated-knowledge-systems-as-downstream-read-models-not-decision-authorities.md)
sets that boundary: generated knowledge systems are downstream read models of
adrkit's human-reviewed decision corpus, never decision authorities.

Tools such as [OpenWiki](https://github.com/langchain-ai/openwiki) can consume
ADRs as evidence and turn them into browsable current-state documentation. That
is complementary to adrkit: the generated wiki is a downstream read model, while
the reviewed records in git retain authority over decision lifecycle and typed
relationships. Machine verification of generated content is not human
ratification of a decision.

See the provisional
[generated-knowledge guide](https://adrkit.dev/generated-knowledge/) for the
OpenWiki setup being evaluated and the ownership boundary ADR-0037 sets between
the two tools.

## Quickstart

The CLI is published as [`@adrkit/cli`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@adrkit/cli)
and exposes the `adr` binary. Published artifacts target **Node 22+**:

```sh
npx @adrkit/cli lint                 # validate the corpus in docs/adr
npx @adrkit/cli explain src/payments/api.ts   # which decisions govern this file?
```

Or add it to a project (Bun-first repos can use `bun add -D @adrkit/cli` / `bunx`):

```sh
npm i -D @adrkit/cli
```

The pure library surfaces install independently:
`npm i @adrkit/core @adrkit/evaluator`.

See the [Quickstart guide](https://adrkit.dev/quickstart/) and the full
[command reference](https://adrkit.dev/commands/).

## Choose a starting point

| If you want to... | Start here | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Validate or inspect an ADR corpus | [`@adrkit/cli`](packages/cli/README.md) | `npx @adrkit/cli ...` on Node 22+ |
| Build your own tooling | [`@adrkit/core`](packages/core/README.md) | Pure parser, validator, matcher, and queue APIs |
| Run the deterministic proposal checks | [`@adrkit/evaluator`](packages/evaluator/README.md) | Pass 0 is the shipped evaluator surface today |
| Feed prior decisions to coding agents | [`@adrkit/mcp`](packages/mcp/README.md) | Local, read-only stdio MCP server |
| Run adrkit from an OCI image | [Container usage](#container-usage) | Lockstep multi-architecture image, beginning with the first release containing ADR-0032 |
| Comment governing decisions on pull requests | [Use in CI](https://adrkit.dev/ci/) | GitHub Action from this repository |
| Browse decisions on GitHub Pages | [Decision portal](https://adrkit.dev/ci/#publish-a-decision-portal-to-github-pages) | Nested build-only Action, beginning with `v0.19.0` |
| Evaluate decision governance with a generated wiki | [Generated knowledge guide](https://adrkit.dev/generated-knowledge/) | Provisional OpenWiki recipe; no runtime coupling |
| Add decision memory to Spec Kit | [`@adrkit/spec-kit`](packages/adapters/spec-kit/README.md) | Published separately for Spec Kit `>=0.13.0,<1.2.0` |
| Add decision memory to Copilot, Claude Code, or opencode | [`adrkit` agent plugin](packages/adapters/agent-plugin/README.md) | Install from this repository or marketplace |

## Container usage

Beginning with the first lockstep release containing
[ADR-0032](docs/adr/0032-publish-one-lockstep-oci-image-after-the-coordinated-release-succeeds.md),
releases are published as a multi-architecture OCI image at
`ghcr.io/mbeacom/adrkit`. Pin an immutable `vX.Y.Z` tag in automation; `vX`
and `latest` move only after that lockstep release has completed:

```sh
docker run --rm --read-only --network none \
  -v "$PWD:/workspace:ro" \
  ghcr.io/mbeacom/adrkit:vX.Y.Z lint

docker run --rm --read-only --network none -i \
  -v "$PWD:/workspace:ro" \
  ghcr.io/mbeacom/adrkit:vX.Y.Z mcp
```

The MCP command keeps stdin open because MCP uses stdio. Its repository mount is
read-only, matching the server contract; use an absolute host path in MCP client
configuration. For CLI commands that intentionally write (`new`, `accept`,
`approve`, `object`, `resolve`, or `migrate` without `--dry-run`), omit
`--read-only` and the mount's `:ro` suffix. The image runs as the non-root
`node` user; on a host with a different UID/GID, add
`--user "$(id -u):$(id -g)"`. On SELinux hosts, add the appropriate
bind-mount label (for example, `:Z`).

The default image treats an unrecognized selector as an `adr` subcommand.
Explicit selectors are `cli`/`adr`/`adrkit`, `mcp`/`adrkit-mcp`,
`server`/`adrkit-server`, `ci`/`adrkit-ci`, and
`queue-action`/`adrkit-queue-action`. The default

readme.markdown:
# UFCalendar Fight API — agent skill

An installable skill that teaches a coding agent how to reach the
[UFCalendar Fight API](https://www.ufcalendar.com/developers) — the MMA Fight Data API
behind our [MCP server for UFC data](https://www.ufcalendar.com/developers/ufc-mcp-server)
and [MMA MCP server](https://www.ufcalendar.com/developers/mma-mcp-server): UFC, PFL,
OKTAGON, BKFC and RIZIN events, full fight cards, results, per-round stats,
fighter careers, judges' scorecards, UFC rankings history since 2013 and
per-country broadcast rights — over REST, the two SDKs, or the MCP server at
`https://api.ufcalendar.com/mcp`.

## Install

```bash
npx skills add UFCalendar/fight-api-skill
```

Or copy it in by hand:

| Agent | Where |
|---|---|
| Claude Code | `.claude/skills/ufcalendar-fight-api/` (project) or `~/.claude/skills/ufcalendar-fight-api/` (global) |
| Cursor | paste `SKILL.md` into a rule under `.cursor/rules/`, keep `references/` beside it |
| Codex | reference `SKILL.md` from `AGENTS.md`, keep `references/` beside it |

The skill is plain Markdown — `SKILL.md` plus four reference files. Nothing
executes.

## Contents

- `SKILL.md` — access in 60 seconds, base URL and envelope, the endpoints that
  answer the common questions, the don'ts, and when to use MCP vs REST vs SDK.
- `references/endpoints.md` — every endpoint and parameter. **Generated** from
  the OpenAPI document; do not edit by hand.
- `references/conventions.md` — envelope, pagination, errors, rate headers,
  tier gates, webhook signature verification.
- `references/mcp-clients.md` — copy-paste config for Claude Code, Cursor,
  Codex, Claude.ai and ChatGPT.
- `references/sdk.md` — Python and TypeScript quickstarts.

## Access

No free tier. A **free 1-day trial** (100 requests, no card, one per account)
self-serves at <https://www.ufcalendar.com/account/api?trial=1>; paid plans
start at $19/month. `GET https://api.ufcalendar.com/v1/plans` answers with no
credential at all, so an agent can evaluate the API before anyone signs in.

Odds are the UFCalendar consensus line only (no book identities; information
only, not betting advice). Fighter images are Creative Commons and
must be shown with their credit. Not affiliated with UFC, Zuffa, TKO or any
promotion.

MIT licensed.

readme.markdown:
# GitHub MCP Server: Teaching an AI to Pick the Right Tool

A read-only **Model Context Protocol** server that lets Claude (or any MCP client) answer questions about
my GitHub repos, issues, pull requests and commits. It comes with a **benchmark** that measures how often
the model picks the right tool with the right arguments.

**Rewriting the tool descriptions took a local 7B model from 63% to 95% correct, and from 60% to 90% on
held-out questions it was never tuned on.** An ablation shows where those 32 points came from, and most of them were not the prose:

| Change | Points | What it was |
|---|---|---|
| Accept bare repo names (`mcp-bench-app`, not only `owner/mcp-bench-app`) | **+17** | input handling in the server |
| Write the range `(1-50)` into the `limit` parameter's description | **+8** | one parameter sentence |
| Rewrite the tool descriptions (when to use, when NOT to, and the alternative) | **+7** | the tool wording |

Every miss left in v2 is the model asking for something the API doesn't offer: merged PRs, sorting by
stars, or closed issues from the open-issues tool. Better wording can't fix those. The next step is to support them in the schema.

**[Explore every question in the results dashboard →](https://abdulmuhaiminkhan.github.io/github-mcp/)**

## What I built

- **MCP server (Python, `mcp` SDK 2.x)** with 6 read-only tools over stdio: `list_repositories`,
  `get_repository`, `list_open_issues`, `search_issues`, `list_pull_requests`, `get_recent_commits`.
- **Least-privilege access:** a fine-grained, read-only GitHub token and `readOnlyHint` annotations.
  The token stays in the server process and never reaches the model.
- **Production behaviour:** schema-validated inputs, retries with backoff and jitter, primary and
  secondary rate-limit handling, ETag caching (304s don't count against the rate limit), exact totals
  for list tools, and error messages that tell the model how to recover.
- **A benchmark with known answers:** a seed script creates two repos with 15 issues, 5 pull requests
  and commits from two authors. A fake GitHub API serves the same data offline, so the benchmark also
  runs in CI with no token.
- **Three evaluations:** tool selection with argument grading (60 questions), a held-out set (20), and
  multi-step agent runs whose final answers are checked against the seeded facts (13).
- **An ablation** (`v1 → v1b → v2`) that separates input handling from description wording.
- **An automatic description optimizer** that rewrites descriptions from failures and keeps a change
  only if held-out accuracy doesn't drop.
- **A harness that benchmarks any MCP server**, not just this one ([examples/](examples/)).
- **A results dashboard** ([docs/](docs/index.html)) with every question, call and error from the runs.
- **Tests and CI** on Python 3.10–3.13 (ruff, mypy, pytest, and an oracle check that the harness
  scores 100% when the right call is made).

## Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    U[User] -->|question| C["Claude Desktop(MCP client)"]
    C <-->|"JSON-RPC over stdiotools/list · tools/call"| S["github-mcpPython MCP server"]
    S -->|"HTTPS · read-only tokenETags · retries"| G[(GitHub REST API)]
    E["eval/run_eval.py"] -.->|"same MCP protocol"| S
    E -.->|"question + tool schemas"| L["LLM under test(Ollama or Claude)"]
    S -.->|"GITHUB_API_URL (CI)"| F[("fake GitHubseeded repos")]
```

| Layer | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `server.py` | Registers tools, validates arguments, returns compact JSON with exact totals |
| `descriptions.py` | Versioned descriptions (`v1` baseline, `v1b` ablation, `v2` optimized, or a JSON file) |
| `github_client.py` | Auth, pagination, retries, rate limits, ETag cache, typed errors |
| `eval/` | Benchmark runner, argument grader, seed script, fake GitHub, optimizer, chart, dashboard export |

## Evaluation

**Method.** Each question goes to the model with the server's own tool list, exactly what Claude
Desktop sends. The harness executes the chosen call through MCP and grades it:

- ✅ **Correct**: expected tool, call succeeded, arguments match (e.g. "last 3 days" → `since_days=3`)
- 🟡 **Wrong Arguments**: right tool, call succeeded, but an argument is wrong or missing
- ⚠️ **Wrong Tool**: a different tool, or no tool
- ❌ **Tool Failed**: right tool, but the call returned an error

There are 60 questions (10 per tool, a third of them in deliberate overlap zones between tools), plus 20
held-out questions written after v2 was frozen and never used for tuning. The data is the seeded
benchmark repos on real GitHub, and the model runs locally with Ollama at temperature 0, 3 runs per
configuration, medians reported. The three runs differed by at most 2 points on the main set and 5 on held-out.

| Configuration (qwen2.5:7b) | Correct | Wrong Arguments | Wrong Tool | Tool Failed | Input tokens |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| v1: vague descriptions | 63% | 0% | 8% | 28% | 614 |
| v1b: v1 + bare repo names | 80% | 0% | 8% | 12% | 614 |
| v2: rewritten descriptions | 95% | 0% | 2% | 3% | 1533 |
| v1 on held-out questions | 60% | 5% | 15% | 20% | 613 |
| v2 on held-out questions | 90% | 0% | 5% | 5% | 1532 |

The offline run against the fake GitHub gave the same picture (65% / 82% / 95%).

**A second model, llama3.1:8b**, same questions and settings:

| Configuration (llama3.1:8b) | Correct | Wrong Arguments | Wrong Tool | Tool Failed | Input tokens |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| v1: vague descriptions | 32% | 7% | 12% | 50% | 643 |
| v1b: v1 + bare repo names | 47% | 7% | 12% | 35% | 643 |
| v2: rewritten descriptions | 92% | 5% | 2% | 2% | 1559 |
| v2 on held-out questions | 95% | 0% | 0% | 5% | 1558 |

Llama picked the right tool 88% of the time even on v1. It failed on arguments: it asked for
`limit=100` on tools capped at 50 again and again, and passed `owner/repo` where a bare name was
expected. The fixes that helped qwen (bare names, the stated limit range) helped llama even more, so the
lesson carries across mo

…

tools.description: 指定した日付(date)の翌日から数えてN営業日目(days)の日付を返します。dateの当日は数えません。daysが負の場合は過去方向（dateの前日から遡ってN営業日目）に計算します。土日・日本の祝日を除外し、calendar="banking"を指定すると銀行休業日（12/31〜1/3）も除外します。dateが営業日かどうかだけ知りたい場合は is_holiday を使ってください（days=0でも同じ情報がskipped経由で得られます）。入力例: {"date": "2026-07-10", "days": 3}

inputs.description: 起点日 YYYY-MM-DD。例: "2026-07-10"。この日自体は数えません。

inputs.name: days
inputs.description: 何営業日先(正)/前(負)かを表す整数。0も指定可: dateをそのまま返し、dateが非営業日ならskippedに1件（date自身とその理由）を記録します。

inputs.description: "standard"（既定）または"banking"（銀行休業日も除外）。

inputs.description: 顧客固有の追加休業日（YYYY-MM-DD の配列）。例: ["2026-12-29", "2026-12-30"]

tools.name: business_days_between
tools.description: from〜to間の営業日数を数えます。既定では「fromを含まず、toを含む」境界です（例:「今日から支払期日まで何営業日か」）。include_from/include_toで境界を変更できます。土日・日本の祝日を除外し、calendar="banking"を指定すると銀行休業日（12/31〜1/3）も除外します。from > to の場合はエラーにせず、from/toとinclude_from/include_toを入れ替えて計算した結果の符号を反転した値（負の営業日数）を返します（反対称則: count(A,B,x,y) = -count(B,A,y,x)。A≠B、すなわちfrom≠toの場合に成立する恒等式で、from===toはこの分岐に入らないため対象外）。入力例: {"from": "2026-07-10", "to": "2026-07-20"}

inputs.name: from
inputs.description: 起点日 YYYY-MM-DD。例: "2026-07-10"。

inputs.name: to
inputs.description: 終点日 YYYY-MM-DD。例: "2026-07-20"。fromより前の日付も指定可（結果は負の営業日数になります）。

inputs.name: calendar
inputs.description: "standard"（既定）または"banking"（銀行休業日も除外）。

inputs.name: extra_closed_dates
inputs.description: 顧客固有の追加休業日（YYYY-MM-DD の配列）。例: ["2026-12-29", "2026-12-30"]

inputs.name: include_from
inputs.description: fromを営業日数に含めるか。既定はfalse。

inputs.name: include_to
inputs.description: toを営業日数に含めるか。既定はtrue。

readme.markdown:
# plugrail

A collection of MCP servers that connect to Japanese public data. The name alone does not describe the project, so plugrail is not related to railways or railway services.

## Live servers

| Server | MCP endpoint | Tools | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| jp-calendar | `https://jp-calendar.plugrail.dev/mcp` | `is_holiday`, `list_holidays`, `business_days_between`, `add_business_days` | Live |

## Connect

See [the jp-calendar connection guide](docs/servers/jp-calendar/CONNECT.md).

## Self-hosting

1. In `packages/servers/jp-calendar/`, copy `wrangler.example.jsonc` to `wrangler.jsonc` and fill in your Cloudflare resource IDs.
2. Create the D1 database and KV namespace referenced by that configuration.
3. Run `pnpm --filter @plugrail/jp-calendar deploy`.

The self-hosted server runs independently. Authentication, rate limiting, and usage metering are features of the hosted service only.

## Architecture

```text
MCP client
    |
    v
jp-calendar Worker --> Cloudflare D1 (holiday data)
                   --> Cloudflare KV (cached data)
```

## Sources and disclaimer

This is not an official service of the National Tax Agency, the Digital Agency, or any other Japanese government body. Information provided does not represent their official views and is not guaranteed by them.

Source: Adapted from the Cabinet Office "National Holidays" page (https://www8.cao.go.jp/chosei/shukujitsu/gaiyou.html)

## Contributing

Issues and pull requests are welcome. Please include enough context to reproduce a problem or explain a proposed change.

## License

MIT. See [LICENSE](LICENSE).
